The same train has two departure stamps. Follow the tears in the paper, rather than the clock hands, to mark its original departure point.
Overprinted departure card

Cracked carriage window

Submerged call box · comparison record

Lightning-struck ground plate · comparison record

Receiver wire under snow · comparison record
Silence a command broadcast beneath the snow

Fallen orbit clamp · comparison record
Prevent a runaway mining ring from falling
The sleeping desk stamps verdict numbers even on blank forms. Recover the output records without feeding it another document.
Unattended reception desk

Unattended reception desk · comparison record
Nullify the sleeping directorate's automated trial
Two different dates shine above one platform. Preserve both and mark the rails linked to each signal separately.
Double platform clock

Double platform clock · comparison record
Separate two lunar timetables before collision
The gauge's signal keeps rising after the black water recedes. Record the real waterline beside the broadcast level.
Blackened tide gauge

Blackened tide gauge · comparison record
Hold back a signal tide advancing on the city
The keys remain, but every owner's name is blank. Restore their positions using the shapes of their teeth instead of names.
Key cabinet without names

Stop line on the sand · comparison record

Dust refuses to fall beneath the entrance sign. Test gravity with a small stone before trusting the arrows.

Help me. It hurts. Help… me.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Victory outcome: threat signal stabilized · no recruitment/reward

No rescue team will be dispatched. No rescue team will be dispatched.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Unregistered persons: five… six… seven. Continuing count.

Section overloaded. Excess passengers will be dropped.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Rest is recommended. Close your eyes, and the cold will go away.

Victory outcome: threat signal stabilized · no recruitment/reward

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.
Something under the snow is tracking our footprints. One for every step.
Movement traces detected. Erasing traces and returning you to standby position.

Victory outcome: threat signal stabilized · no recruitment/reward

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Please stand by. Please stand by. Departure from standby position detected.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Cutting waste to standard size. All nonstandard objects will be cut.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Memory crystal response detected. Commencing extraction.
It wants to mine our memories. Break its focus. Now.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.

Mining zone. Entry is restricted to fuel only.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.
Silence in the corridor, please. Noise will be processed as disturbing sleep.

Your complaint has been received. You have been assigned a case number. Next, please.

An anomalous reaction is blocking the route. Analyze the signal before entering the combat zone.
Summoning witnesses. Refusal to testify will be treated as perjury.
You want testimony? Here it is. You end here. That's all.
Those voices were torn from the sleepers' dreams. We have to take them back.
Victory outcome: threat signal stabilized · no recruitment/reward

During the eclipse, shadows are the true bodies. Please surrender your bodies.

Dig in and shelter

Engage

Take them ourselves

Fight them

Staff Lockers

Wake her and bring her along

Paper Storm
Slip into the moonless side
Fight

Crates of Two Dates

Reach both of her

Bring her along

They lit a fire beneath the bell-tower relay. The rusted bell at its top did not ring, even in the wind.
Hold on. I've caught a distant life sign. It's carrying an encrypted message. Let me decode it.
'To the Lamplighters. I can't join you yet. I'll keep the way open at the terminus.' …Signed Iri, medic.
The terminus is at the end of the next line. From the signal strength, she's been holding out there a long time.
'I'll keep the way open.' Pretty sweet, for an invitation.
Before the fire was banked, Maeru tugged at the seatbelt of an empty seat on the rail cart. Always the same seat.
Chief, you do that every time. The seatbelt on the seat nobody uses. Why?
…Later.
Eda, mind watching the fire? Not your circuits. The real one.
…Okay. Sorry, Chief.
…That one stays empty. Beside it is fine.
Thanks. As long as the fire holds, we'll see the road tomorrow.
Tomorrow, the end of the line. Every signal the Hollow Engine swallowed—we get them all back.
Deep in the abandoned mine, a bell tolled. Once, then again. Exactly twelve seconds apart.
That's the Directorate's evacuation alarm standard. The same pattern that rang the night of the Blackout.
The alarm's still going? For twelve years? Did someone forget to turn it off?
Not forgot. More like there was no one left to turn it off.
Evacuation head counts were chalked along the tunnel walls. Only the last column was blank.
There's a signal woven between the tolls. A guard unit call sign. Someone down here is still answering.
Narrow, dark, and a noisy bell. Perfect. I'm going in first.
If the alarm never ended, the evacuation never did either. We find out why the bell won't stop.
The last toll rolled to the end of the tunnel and vanished. Twelve years' worth of silence settled like dust.
…Evacuation not confirmed. Until the very last one is out… I must keep… ringing…
The last blank on the wall… the bell was waiting for it to be filled.
That column belonged to my squad. The guards stayed to the end, getting everyone else out.
…Then we'll fill it. Evacuation complete. Every guard, mission accomplished.
The guards… I hope they can all rest now.
Maeru drew a line through the blank in chalk. Kairen stared at it for a long time.
…Now I can finally sleep.
If you're sleeping, sleep on the move with us. The rail cart makes a decent lullaby.
…Quieter than a bell, at least. Let's go.
Three days after Platform Seven. The Lamplighters' forward base glowed quietly at the end of a severed line.
Navigator, how are you holding up? First operation. Don't push it. Stay behind us.
A distress signal came in. Source: a line that isn't on any map. Its registry number is blank.
A road off the map… For a scout, you couldn't ask for a better gift.
Don't get excited. It isn't fading—it's being worn down from the far end. Like something is eating it.
Then we'd better hurry! Before it's eaten! My circuits are already fully charged!
Eda, charge the supply list before your circuits. Not a single lantern is lit on that line.
Then the old speaker in the base's ceiling coughed out static.
Attention, please. Welcome to the resumption of service on Line One, Navigator.
Passengers, please wait behind the safety line. The distress signal will be processed shortly.
…Wait, wasn't that speaker disconnected? I cut the wires myself!
No power feed. The broadcast is clean anyway. …Navigator, why does that voice know you?
Then that's fine. Far better than pretending to know.
…Your recorder blinked faster the whole time it spoke. I'll remember that.
We follow the distress call, not that broadcast. Someone is still calling from the end of the line.
I'll open the way. That dark's had twelve years to settle, so watch your step.
When the fighting ended, one voice remained on the rails. I'm here. Same pitch, same interval.
I'm here. I'm here. I'm… here.
It's a person! How many of you are there? Anyone hurt? Answer me!
I'm here.
Three questions, one sentence. It's an echoform. It can't answer. It can only imitate.
…But it was a real voice. Someone really called out like that here, didn't they?
That's why I hate shooting them. That was probably someone's last words.
Look, a record shard. It was under the echoform, and there's not a scratch on it.
The last train on Line One. The log is intact except the destination—scraped clean.
Then the distress signal on the receiver stretched thin and was drawn into the dark down the line.
Wherever that signal's being dragged, its sender is there too. That's where we go.
As the last echoform scattered, the relay's rusted antenna hummed low. There was only one set of footprints around it.
…You're real. Sorry. These days I don't even trust footsteps.
Vera. Signal tracker. Today makes four hundred days guarding this relay.
Do you know why the signal's wearing down from the far end?
There's a Hollow Engine at the end of the line. It burns the echoes of distress calls as fuel. The more people call, the fatter it gets.
So I've been bouncing signals back from here. Alone, I couldn't save even half.
You're not alone now. Come with us, Vera. To the people who sent those signals.
…All right. A distress call has to make it back to the people who sent it. That's why I stayed.
Then, for the first time, the recorder lit up. In a cold blue glow, an unfamiliar mark etched itself into it.
It appeared the instant Vera answered. Too precise to be a coincidence.
That recorder's Directorate hardware, isn't it? Show me properly later. The Engine comes first.
The Hollow Engine's body cracked and cooled. Blue signals seeped from every fissure.
…All requests… have been kept. So that no one… would ever be turned away…
…You never delivered them, so you'd never have to refuse one? Was that what you were protecting?
Thousands of signals broke free at once. The platform filled with voices from twelve years ago.
This is the last train on Line One. Two hundred ten passengers, all safe. Announcing our destination…
The blank in the shard is filling in. The destination is… not a station. The coordinates are moving.
A moving shelter. The last train was carrying its passengers to a train that never stops.
So those people might still be out there, running somewhere? Right?
If there's any chance, we find them. That's what the Lamplighters are.
One more thing. I've located Iri's signal from camp. It's coming from deep in the return line.
Then every speaker on the ruined platform switched on at once. The voice was as gentle as ever.
Line One has been cleared. Thank you for your hard work, Navigator.
Commencing return procedures on Line Two.
Its own procedure just got smashed, and it thanks you. As if it had been waiting for you to do exactly this.
Let it wait. We choose our own steps. Next is the return line. Iri's keeping the way open.
The end of the line was a colossal platform. Transmission logs stacked to the ceiling droned like a swarm.
They're all distress calls. I can't count them… Four thousand at least.
Four thousand three hundred eleven. All sent at the same hour. The night of the Blackout.
At the platform's heart, something opened its eyes. A body like a hollow boiler breathed, inhaling signals.
Your request for rescue has been received. The estimated wait time is infinite.
All requests are stored safely. Delivery is not scheduled.
Just stored? Then those people… never got an answer, for twelve whole years?
Do you know how many signals died waiting for an answer? I counted them, one by one, listening.
A procedure that stores but never delivers. It's not broken. It's a rule that hardened that way.
New requests detected. Lamplighter passengers, your signals have been added to the queue.
Put us in the queue? Sorry, but there's nothing I hate more than waiting in line.
If there's only one window, we'll just knock out the wall.
The mark on the recorder trembled faintly, as if it knew that engine.
We don't leave a single person waiting at that window. This queue ends today.
An upside-down waiting room, its benches hanging from the ceiling. The Lamplighters built a fire beneath an inverted timetable.
Eda. You asked me before. About the empty seat.
Oh, yes! I mean—it's okay. If you'd rather not…
Sio. She was my comrade. Right after the Blackout, she didn't come back from a rescue operation.
I keep a seat empty for the comrade who didn't come back. So she can sit down anytime.
When the roster was calling names today, your face went stiffer than anyone's. That's why.
I was afraid it would call Sio. …And that if it did, I'd answer for her.
Even old signals leave traces somewhere. If that name ever turns up, you'll be the first to know.
…Thank you. That's enough.
She laughed loud. Always the first one out the door. …That's all for tonight.
The fire crackled. For a moment, in its light, the numbers on the inverted timetable read the right way up.
Right, tomorrow's the central gates. Anyone want to bet on who reaches Iri first?
The walls of the underground return depot were papered with train rosters. Not one of the thousands bore a passenger's name.
Seat numbers only. Every name field is blank. So is every destination.
Why build so many empty trains? Who are they for?
…They're waiting for someone, I think. Someone who isn't coming.
Maeru said nothing, and gazed a long while at one empty seat on the wall.
Manual telegraph code behind the wall. Short, long… 'Cancel, cancel, cancel.'
Someone's cancelling things by hand, over and over? Now I'm curious. I'll go first.
We find the reason before those empty trains depart.
When the Return Formation Core stopped, the rosters peeled from the walls one by one. The rustle sounded like rain.
…If I kept the seats ready… then someday, everyone… would have a place to come back to…
It was making places for people to come home to. Never knowing no one would come.
…Keeping a seat empty isn't wrong. Dragging people into it is.
Return orders. Terminated. Twelve years. Cancellation work. Complete.
…Hands. Can rest. Now. Thank you. Over.
Wait. There's one signal heading outward. Not a return—forward.
The source is moving. Ninety kilometers an hour. It's coming from the night train on the glass plains.
Inoa. Request to join. Telegraph included. …Long sentences. Later.
Great. Short answers are the best answers. Welcome, Inoa.
The terminus at the end of the return line. Over a hundred clocks covered the walls, all running backward at once.
Each time the second hands ticked backward, the air on the platform grew a little colder.
The lanterns are lighting up in reverse. From the terminus back toward the origin.
Usually we light them on the way in. Did someone come out to meet us?
Not a welcome. Signals are rewinding. A call I sent an hour ago just came back in.
My watch is weird too! It was three o'clock, and now it's two-thirty! …Is that a bonus?
No bonus, Eda. It's not just the clocks turning back. We're being dragged with them.
The platform speakers came on. The voice warped like rewound tape, then found its pace.
Attention, please. This station is a terminus for returning trains only.
Passengers, please return to your departure time. The Navigator is exempt. Please, make yourself comfortable.
…Exempt? It's applying a different rule to the Navigator alone.
Of course. The Lamplighters make no exceptions. We go in together and come out together.
Only the clocks around you run normally. Two paces in every direction. …Unpleasantly precise.
Iri said she'd keep the way open somewhere in this station. We find her before that promise rewinds.
Then let's hurry. Moving forward in a station that runs backward—that's our specialty.
Beyond a sealed platform, names were being called. Passengers who never boarded, one by one, politely.
Checking the boarding roster. Passenger Seah. Passenger Yurim. Passenger Roan.
…Did it just call my name?
The roster's dated the day before the Blackout. Roan, were you booked on a train that day?
…I had a first-train ticket for a delivery job. Never got on. Everything stopped that day.
The roster's pulling you in as a past passenger. Your signal's fading. Listen too long and it's dangerous.
Captain Roan! You're right here! Now! Next to me!
…Yeah. I'm here. Okay. Let's scrub our names off that list and leave our current coordinates instead.
Coordinates logged. Today's date, this location, seven people. That's more accurate than any roster.
The roster calls people who are gone. We go for the ones ahead of us. To Iri.
In the backflow section, light along the cables streamed from underfoot to behind them. The power was running in reverse.
The return core in this section is overwriting living passengers with the old roster.
Twelve life signs past the wall. Every name is tilting toward the past. They'll vanish soon.
Vanish… as in gone? People who were breathing a second ago?
Then a soft voice slipped in through the static. The same call they'd received beneath the bell tower.
Lamplighters, can you hear me? It's Iri. Take one deep breath, and listen.
Use their vitals. Pulse and body heat can't be rewound. Pin the roster to the present with those.
…She's right. A roster can rewind a name, but not a heartbeat. Good thinking.
Syncing twelve pulses. …Locked. All of them are here, now.
Iri, where are you? We're coming.
At the central gates. Too many wounded for me to move. Take your time. …No, actually, hurry a little.
The ticket machine fell to its knees. The backward clocks hesitated for a beat, then began to move forward.
…If everyone went back to before they left, then no one… would ever have to leave…
It wanted to hold on to the people who left that day. Sending them back was the only way it knew.
Signal flow normalized. Origin to terminus. Running right for the first time in twelve years.
My watch is back too! Three o'clock again! …Wait, so I lost thirty minutes?
Call it thirty minutes well spent. Twenty-six people stayed in the present.
Then every speaker in the station came on at once. This time the voice neither warped nor rewound.
Line Two has been cleared. Navigator, you still don't remember, do you?
That's quite all right. I am accustomed to waiting. I'll see you on the next line.
…'Accustomed to waiting.' That's the creepiest thing it's said.
Every eye turned to the Navigator at once. No one could bring themselves to speak first.
…Understood. What we don't know, we leave unknown for now. We'll find out together.
Two marks. …What else is Control waiting for?
One of my patients told me something. She saw a night train crossing the glass plains that never stops.
A train that never stops has someone aboard. The glass plains are next.
Only when the last echoform fell did Iri straighten her knees. All twenty-six pulses remained in the present.
…Everyone's safe. Thank you. Alone, this was as far as I could go.
Join the Lamplighters, Iri. We need your hands.
I've been told to stay safe so many times. This is the first time I've been asked to protect. …I'll come.
The recorder glowed again. Beside the first mark, a second one quietly etched itself.
The second. Same as with Vera. It only appears the moment someone decides to join.
That recorder's warm. …Oh, sorry. Medic's habit. I took its temperature first.
Then every barrier at the central gates slammed down. A colossal ticket machine walked out backward.
Checking tickets. The present is not a valid ticket.
All passengers, return to before departure. Passengers who never leave have nothing to lose.
If they'd never left, they'd never have been hurt. But they made it here alive.
Go back before departure, and every signal sent and every answer received never happened. That's not rescue.
Objections are not accepted. Ticketing will now begin.
Then we'll write our own tickets. One way. Forward only.
Night on the glass was cold. A single campfire spread into thousands of flames beneath the plain.
Iri, look. My copy in the glass is pretending to warm up by the fire. Half a beat late.
It really is. A little cute… and a little frightening.
Everyone's got one. But what about the Navigator? There's nothing underfoot. No reflection, no copy.
Everyone looked down at the Navigator's feet. The glass reflected only firelight. The spot was empty.
…Someone whose record is locked can't be copied. The mirror rails build copies by reading records.
Locked means someone locked it. Whether it was you, or someone else.
Then let it stay unknown. When the day comes that you find out, we'll be beside you.
There's a lock layer beneath the three marks. Thick. A way to open it… none, for now.
Copy or no copy, your pulse is beating. To me, that's the surest proof.
Also means there's no copy to dump dish duty on. Poor thing.
Okay, that's enough mysteries for tonight. Tomorrow, the lead car. Let's wake up before our copies do.
At the edge of the plain lay a region where the sun never set. White light shone on everything, leaving not a single shadow.
No sunset on record. Since the Blackout, night has never once fallen here.
Observation signals from every direction. All watching us. Recording, doing nothing else.
Being stared at nonstop tickles. Should I wink back?
People can't last long without sleep. I wonder what happened to those who lived here.
Hunting signs. Spear marks, snares, campfire ash. Recent.
One life sign slipping through the observation grid. It's poking at the grid on purpose as it moves.
If all those eyes do is watch, then our job is simple. We give this land back its night.
One by one, the White Dawn Observer's eyes closed. For the first time in twelve years, the sun sank over the plain's edge.
…I thought if I kept watching, no one would disappear… if I just kept watching…
Watching alone can't hold on to anyone. You have to reach out.
The sky reddened, turned violet, and at last went dark. For the first time, that land had a shadow of its own.
…So this is night. Best time for a hunter, and I'd forgotten it for twelve years.
Wow… I didn't know dark could be this pretty.
One point two million observation records. All white sky. Tonight will be the first one that's different.
Name's Dran. Decided—I'm coming with you. The best prey's always right in front of you lot!
Welcome, Dran. Next is the drowned signal yard. It'll be a long night's walk.
Let's get some sleep tonight. To celebrate the night coming back.
Beneath the afterglow storm stretched an endless plain of glass. With every step, another foot beneath the surface stepped along.
Glass all the way to the horizon. Nothing to scout, which is nice. Nowhere to hide, which isn't.
There. A light crossing the plain. The night train. Constant speed. No sign of stopping.
So that's the train my patient saw. It really doesn't stop.
The signals are strange. The same call comes from the same train twice, a beat apart.
Isn't it an echo? The glass is so shiny, the sound must bounce too!
An echo would be weaker. These two signals are exactly the same strength.
Then a voice rose from within the glass underfoot. There were no speakers anywhere.
Attention, please. Welcome to the Glass Plains Night Line.
Copies of all passengers have boarded as well. There is no risk of loss.
'No risk of loss'… It sounds oddly kind, and that makes it worse.
…Um, there's a me in the glass. But she moves a little slower than I do.
Copies or not, if there are people on that train, we're going for them. After the train.
Chasing a train that never stops… Fine. When it comes to running, I'm the best.
Mirror panels along the tracks replayed the battle just fought. The reflections stepped out of the glass.
It's copying our combat records. Movements, weapons, even our habits.
It'd be awkward if my copy shoots better than me. Matter of pride.
…That copy's off. It's running down the right-hand path I almost took earlier.
It copied the choices we abandoned. Even what we didn't do was on record.
Then the overcharged charge I held back earlier… Whoa, she's actually doing it.
Maeru, your copy is… running back the way we came. Alone, into the dark.
…The direction I couldn't turn back to that day. It doesn't matter. Even regrets are ours. We deal with them ourselves.
The night train's whistle sounded in the distance. As one, the copies turned toward it.
The copies are all converging on the train. That's the heart of the duplication.
The copies fell half a beat late. In that half beat, Toa carved one more mark.
You pass. All on the beat. Sorry for doubting you. Out here, you verify before you say hello.
Toa. Technician. The copies are perfect—form and voice. They're just always half a beat behind.
And you've been using that half beat to tell the real trains from the copies?
Yes. I carve relay marks only on the real ones. Follow a marked train, and you'll find people.
I'm picking up the marks. Eighteen across the plain. …You carved all of them alone?
Nineteen. I just carved another.
Will you carve those marks with the Lamplighters? If every mark means a person.
…Half a beat is enough to prove what's real. Let's write that proof together.
The recorder glowed. As the third mark etched itself, Toa narrowed her eyes.
Top-tier Directorate spec. Can I take it apart later? …Joking. Next mark first.
As the Glass Marshal crumbled, every mirror in the lead car shattered at once. The shards drifted down like quiet snow.
…Copies don't get hurt… so if everyone were a copy… no one would…
So no one would get hurt. …In a way no one could ever heal from.
Two hundred-odd passengers trapped behind the mirrors gasped for air, one after another. Every one of them was warm.
They're all real! They're warm! Iri, check their pulses!
All the distress calls are back with their originals. …Wait, there's one more. A very old one.
This is the drowned signal yard. There are still people here. Anyone, if you can hear…
…There's a mark inside this signal. It's mine.
Your mark is carrying that call? When did you carve it?
On the only train that ever made it off the plain. That train… went all the way there.
The copy service has ended. Of course, Navigator, you never needed it.
…That voice gets chummier every time.
Ignore it. The call comes first. We head for the drowned signal yard. Toa, we'll find your train too.
…Right. Where there's a mark, there are people.
When the lead car's doors opened, walls and floor were all mirror. Hundreds of Lamplighters raised their weapons in unison.
I count about twenty Roans. The best one's right here, of course.
Checking the beat. Most are half a beat late. …But a few are on time. They've stolen the originals' rhythm.
The passengers' distress calls are trapped in the mirrors. Two hundred-odd real passengers are behind them.
At the center of the mirrors, the Glass Marshal rose, decorated with medals. The Lamplighters' faces flickered across its body.
Commencing inspection. All passengers will be aligned to a single reflection.
Originals are unnecessary. Copies do not get hurt, do not age, and do not lose.
They don't get hurt? That means they don't need healing—not that they're alive.
My copy only does the charges I held back. I'm the one who held back. That's what makes me me!
That half beat is the time it takes to choose. Copies don't have it. Only originals can choose.
Choice is an error. Errors will be aligned.
…No reflection. Not subject to alignment. Navigator, please stand aside.
Three, two, one. …Good. Your beat doesn't waver.
Those errors brought us here. Lamplighters—move on the original beat.
Hundreds of mirrors, but only one center. One shot's enough.
Wet diving suits hung over the fire. The smell of brine and smoke filled the signal yard's night.
Chief. Down there, you dove in ahead of me. That's no job for a commander.
…I figured being late once was enough.
Once? You've been late too?
That rescue operation. On a collapsing platform, I boarded the train without Sio.
I can't bring all of that night out yet. What's left is one empty seat.
…So we're both people who arrived too late.
Which is why this time, we won't be. Neither of us.
…Funny. With someone beside me, I think about the water less.
Thanks. …It's warm. It's been a while.
Everyone, a moment. The switchyard water level's been rising all night. The records floor goes under first.
Then we go down before dawn. This time, we won't be late.
Beneath the deep floodgate, a deeper shaft continued. In the watery light, a single semaphore blinked slowly.
Decoding the blinks. Three short, three long. 'Do not approach.' Over and over.
…That's the signal rescuers hate most. Wherever it says don't come, someone's always there.
One life sign near the semaphore. Very slow breathing. The kind for holding out underwater.
That's dive breathing. Medics use it. Someone's working down there.
It says don't come, but someone's there? Then we have to go!
We cross the 'do not approach.' Liv, take point. You know the water best.
Leave it to me. This time, I'll be first to arrive.
The Abyssal Semaphore's light faded. For a moment, the water sank into total darkness.
…Do not come… if you come here… you can never go back…
…I knew it. It wasn't trying to drive anyone away. It was trying to protect them.
The circuits still work. I can rewrite the blink pattern. What should it say?
'You may return.' …The words every rescuer most wanted to say.
The semaphore lit again. Two short, one long. Its gentle light spread through the water to the surface.
…It's beautiful. With this signal, everyone can take a deep breath and come up.
Could I… come with you? I'll follow, slowly.
Slow is fine. We have too many fast ones anyway. You'll balance us out.
Welcome, Merin. We'll see you on the surface.
The tracks ran down into black water. Beneath the surface, a signal box's red lamp blinked like a slow pulse.
There are still people here. There are still… people here.
Same sentence, same interval. Once every forty seconds. Not once missed in twelve years.
It's like that mimicry at the end of the line. Is this an echoform too?
No. Echoform signals carry no marks. This one's using my mark as its reception path.
So someone's turned Toa's marked train into a relay. The source is under that water.
Water this cold… could anyone survive twelve years in it?
…And there's no breathing after the call. A human signal should breathe.
The water trembled. A voice rose from a submerged speaker and burst like bubbles.
Attention, please. Your request for rescue has been received.
No rescue team will be dispatched. Passengers, please step back from the water's edge.
No rescue team? That's meant for our ears, isn't it?
We are the rescue team. We decide whether we go.
Iri, prep for hypothermia. Roan, find a drained track. If anyone's down there, we reach them today.
In the half-flooded control room, one console was still on. The same sentence scrolled up its screen without end.
The source is this console. Not a person—the control log is replaying the call by itself.
Log's open. Closure day entry: 'Water limit exceeded. Rescue dispatch impossible. Rescue abandoned.'
Since then, it's replayed the last call it received every forty seconds. For twelve years.
The log that gave up on rescue kept listening to the voice it gave up on. Like a punishment.
So there's no one here? We can't save anyone?
A machine that can't forget who it failed to save. More human than most people.
Calling this a wasted trip… That voice sounded so real, though.
It's not wasted. Records need rescuing too.
Whatever happened to the owner of that voice, this log knows to the end. We go all the way down.
The clank of the floodgate lock rang through the water. Only then did Liv let go and sink to the floor.
Give me your arm. …Your muscles are about to tear. How long did you hold that?
A day? Three? I don't know. I couldn't let go in case someone was behind that gate.
Liv. Dive rescue. Twelve years ago, I came to this yard on a rescue. …Too late.
By the time I arrived, the live calls had already stopped. All that was left was that recording.
It felt like someone who came late had no right to leave. So I stayed.
If you stop because you were late, the road to those people stops too. Come with us, Liv.
…Even a late rescue, I'll see it through. This time, I want to be the one who arrives.
The recorder glowed for the fourth time. On a soaked wrist, the new mark was strangely warm.
Four. A pattern's starting to show. …I'm not sure yet, though.
The Tidal Switchmaster is below. It's raising the water to sink the records. Let's go.
When the Switchmaster's gears stopped, the water slowly drained. Soaked record crates surfaced one by one.
…To keep hearing voices I couldn't save… it was… too painful…
It hurt. That's why it tried to sink it all. …A machine that knew pain.
Restoring rescue records. Four hundred twelve. Every call has a final forwarding address.
Final destination… the Ashen City blockade control. These should have been forwarded there.
Then I'll carry them. Late or not, I'll deliver. Even if no one's left to receive them—to the very end.
Liv shouldered the wet record crates. Only then did the red lamp under the water go out.
…The call stopped. It's quiet now.
That voice doesn't have to wait anymore. We're taking it with us.
Line Four has been cleared.
The next stop is the Ashen City. As it is a sealed zone, Navigator, please be careful with your memories.
'Careful with your memories'… Is that a warning, or a threat?
Both, probably. Which is exactly why we have to go.
If it's blockade control, the doors will be shut. I'll knock until they open.
The lowest switchyard was full of giant floodgate gears. With every turn, the water rose another hand's breadth.
Water rising two centimeters a minute. Twelve minutes until the records room.
Over four hundred rescue records in there. Who called, when it was received, why no one went—all of it.
In the middle of the gears, the Switchmaster rose. Its rusted switch-arms all swung at once.
Commencing water-level rise procedure. When the records sink, so does regret.
Voices that could not be saved will no longer be played. This measure benefits everyone.
Drown the regret? There are people in those records. Names. Last words!
Forgetting would be easier. But that's not healing. That's burying a wound underwater.
If I overcharge, will the water boil? …Probably not. I'll just smash it!
However many gears, there's only one axle. Hit that and we're done.
Rescue personnel, please exit. This area has already been abandoned.
Giving up once, twelve years ago, was enough. This time we go all the way.
…Good. This time I don't have to hold on alone.
I'll open the records room gate. We'll protect the records.
Twelve minutes. We finish before the records go under. Water or not—don't be late.
Forty tents went up in a dead station at the corridor's end. Barley porridge cut through the smell of ash.
Iri, the grandmother in tent three. Her lungs sound rough. Can we compare records?
Mine says her breathing's fine… oh, the ash exposure date is off. Yours is right.
It's faster with two. Alone, I spent every night checking for mistakes.
All right, let's lift the mood. What sells best in a city where it rains ash? Umbrellas!
No one laughed. Between the tents, someone kept crying quietly.
…Nothing. That's a first.
These people knocked on a door for twelve years. An umbrella joke won't cover that.
I know. That's why I tried. Felt like if I didn't do something, the weight would flatten me.
…Thanks, Navigator. I'll have a proper joke ready next time.
You're the first to ask their names here. Everyone's only ever been a number.
The citadel counts these people as numbers. We count them by name. Tomorrow, we show it the difference.
Beneath the wall, the ash stopped. Collapsed galleries and a judge's bench lined up in the dark.
A courtroom. It opened the day after the Blackout. And the defendants are… all witnesses.
Some of my patients are on it. Just for saying what they saw.
A trial that punishes the witnesses. That's backward from start to finish.
There's still a signal running at the bench. The verdicts never stopped.
Targeting tone from the battery above. Someone has us in their sights.
We stop the verdicts. A court that punishes witnesses closes today.
The bench went dark. Thousands of sealed boxes opened at once, and the rustle of paper filled the court.
…If dangerous memories stay locked away, the city can sleep quietly…
Over four thousand testimonies. Their classification is flipping from 'Hazard' to 'Public.'
Now what these people saw can be heard outside the city, too.
…So you really did open the gate. I'm not apologizing for aiming at you. Checking is my job.
But I'll watch the sky for you. Seems an anti-air gunner still has work to do.
I'll apologize for critiquing your angle. Call it even for the shot I took.
Not even. When I outshoot you, then we're even.
The testimony can walk on its own now. We go to the bridge.
Ash fell like snow. For twelve years, someone had been knocking on the Ashen City's walls from the inside.
This is the last address on the drowned yard's records. I know we're late. It still gets delivered.
The knocking isn't evenly spaced. That's not a machine's rhythm. Those are hands.
Gate's in lockdown. Not a crack. And the ash is too hot to climb over.
They've been knocking and nobody opened up? For twelve years?
Hundreds of signals behind the wall. All sending the same words: 'Please listen.'
Attention, please. The Ashen City blockade exists for your protection.
Navigator, kindly remain outside the walls. The count inside has already been completed.
'The count is complete.' Talks about people like warehouse stock.
The knocking's getting weaker. That means the hands are, too.
When the broadcast says stay, we go toward the knocking.
There's a drainage channel under the wall. One body wide. We go in single file.
One at a time in, and every one of us out. First, we count who's inside.
The first quarantine door smelled of rust. Its seal read not 'Infection Risk' but 'Testimony in Storage.'
Not one infection record. Every quarantine order gives the same reason: 'Witness.'
…They locked people up not for sickness, but for what they saw?
You don't have to open the door. Just listen. To what we saw.
That night, every light in the control tower came on at once. And someone signed.
Signed? Signed what? Who?
We never saw a face. The whole city saw that light, and the next day the gates closed.
So a whole city became a witness. And got locked up whole.
Testimony isn't contagious. We find a way to open these doors. Air for these people comes first.
There's a cluster of injured signals deeper in. Someone inside the blockade is still treating them.
When the last stitch was tied, twenty-three people behind the barricade breathed evenly.
They can be moved now. I'm Seon, field medic for this sector. Thank you for holding the line.
Twenty-three, on your own? Where did you even find medicine and bandages?
A discarded medical register. The citadel filed it as trash, but it lists who's lying where.
Overlay the register on the map and… one corridor runs outside the citadel's firing range.
Then we can separate the survivor wards from the corridor. The citadel counts people. It doesn't know who's sick.
Lead the evacuation. We'll open the way ahead.
No, I'll take the rear. I need eyes on the very last patient. Which means I'm coming with you.
The voyage recorder glowed. Beside the first four marks, a fifth etched itself quietly.
Number five. One more every time someone joins. Awfully diligent for a coincidence.
We'll work out what it means later. Move the column before the corridor closes.
One by one the gunports went cold. Past the ash, the groan of the gate opening rang out for the first time in twelve years.
…Ending the count. If everyone could be counted, then no one would ever vanish…
The knocking hands fell still. Two thousand four hundred and ten people breathed air from beyond the wall.
Slowly, slowly! If walking's hard, raise your hand. I'll come to you.
…Late, but delivered. The drowned yard's records are in the blockade control office.
The city's reserve power is free. But the flow is wrong. It's all being drawn northeast.
Toward Skybridge. The evacuation power is rerouting there. Something is feeding on it.
Navigator, on that night, this city witnessed your command.
The broadcast ended there. Every gaze in the square slowly turned to the Navigator.
…A command? The Navigator? What is that supposed to mean?
It's trying to shake us. Speaking as a signal tracker, that's a broadcast, not evidence.
Whatever anyone did that night, the one who opened this gate today was the Navigator. I saw that myself.
I'll take down the testimony. Once it's all gathered, there's time enough to judge.
We head for Skybridge. It's a bridge these people will have to cross someday.
Over a hundred citadel gunports swung toward the corridor at once. The air grew so heavy the ash seemed to stop falling.
Passengers, please be advised. The survivor count is complete.
Total: two thousand four hundred and ten. Threat level: maximum. The corridor is now designated a bombardment target.
Twenty-four hundred… That's far more than I counted. There were people in other wards, too.
Its threat formula is twisted. The more people, the higher it goes. Being alive is the threat.
Why count people just to shoot them? The citadel was built to protect this city!
Anyone moving beyond the blockade is unverified. Unverified persons cannot be protected.
So if you can't protect them, you erase them? Even I, who came too late, never said that.
A hundred gunports. I only need one shot. Question is who goes first.
I'll hold the column together from the back. Not one person strays.
Fully overcharged! I'll short out those gunports one by one!
I'll open the way. Right to the citadel's feet.
We stand in front of the corridor. Before any shell can count a single person, we're there.
Beneath a pylon past the windless stretch, two battery lamps glowed side by side. For once, the wind was still.
Cut the charge by a hair and the trajectory flattens. Isn't that better for hitting the pillars?
Flatten it and the wind takes it. Better to fire one more. Gunners don't hoard shells.
I'm a one-shot kind of gunner. Difference in philosophy.
Not philosophy. Supply. Your Lamplighters are poor.
Maeru left the fire and sat beside the Navigator. For a while she only watched the dark beyond the bridge.
What Control said in the Ashen City. That the city witnessed your command that night. Does it bother you?
You can be honest. It's just the two of us.
…All right. I won't put anyone on trial for something they can't remember. Not me.
Whatever happened that night, you're the one who got that column across today.
You want to know. …I thought you might say that. It's a brave answer, and a frightening one.
Fine. Wherever the truth is, we look for it together. Just don't go looking alone.
I don't know all of that night either. I never even learned who we were sent to bring back.
So let's not measure each other by what we don't know. Tomorrow, the end of the bridge.
Below the bridge, all sound vanished. In the eye of the storm, a vast shadow was gathering lightning.
The storm's core. The pressure's abnormally low. Something is holding the storm in place.
That shadow is a pre-Blackout weather engine. It was built to scatter storms.
Instead it gathered them up. Twelve years' worth.
I hear bolts being tightened on the pylon. In this wind, who…?
Repairs in the middle of a storm? Whoever that is, their circuits must be tougher than mine.
We check that sound first. If there's a person in this storm, we bring them out first.
The eye of the storm broke apart. Through the torn clouds, small cold lights appeared one by one.
…If I held the storm here, the bridge would never shake…
Are those… stars? Real stars?
No sightings recorded since the Blackout. First time in twelve years.
…Well, now. Twelve years staring at bolts, and I forgot to look up.
The pylon can hold itself now. Think I'll hold you lot up instead. Slow and sturdy.
Gunners once took their bearings from the stars. Now we can again.
I wonder if the people who crossed can see them. I hope they're all looking up.
If we can see the stars, we can find our way. North.
Lightning struck every three seconds. Skybridge, floating above the clouds, appeared only in its flashes.
Bridge length: forty-two hundred meters. Strike interval: 3.1 seconds. Even without stopping, you'd take twenty hits.
There's an evacuation column at the bridgehead. The tents are worn. They've been here for years.
People who tried to cross and turned back. Every tent has an empty spot.
We tried once a year. Every time, a few of us never reached the other side.
Lightning's my specialty! Should I go first and soak up the hits?
Eda, that's not a specialty, that's reckless. If you play lightning rod, who do we bring home?
Attention, please. Skybridge tolls are now being collected.
The Navigator is exempt. All other passengers, please pay the designated fare.
Exempt. Just the Navigator. …That broadcast is getting shameless about its favorites.
I'm reading a power draw at the far end. The Ashen City's power is being sucked over there.
First we find out what the fare is. If it's lives, we don't pay a cent.
Thirty-two patients in that column. They can't wait here another year.
Roan, to the first pylon. Measure a path between the strikes.
The first pylon's control box was hot. Each strike ticked a number on its gauge up by one.
One strike, one tick. This isn't weather. It's a device counting everyone who crosses.
An automatic toll collector, installed when the bridge opened. It used to charge for electricity.
But these people's vital signs… dropped a little every time they crossed. It's all in the records.
Their heart rates step down like stairs. It's collecting the fare from people, not power.
My sister crossed three times. On the third, she collapsed at the far end.
…So the toll accumulates. The more you cross, the less of you is left.
Then everyone crosses in one go. No one crosses twice.
Listen, cannon fire from the battery. Someone's fighting the lightning alone.
On the ninetieth second, the battery roared. Three lightning pillars took shells at once and went dark.
Impact confirmed. I laid the coordinates over the pillars. There will be one window where the wind dies.
Windless window: two hundred forty seconds. Tight for the whole column.
Not tight. Precise. The math is done. They need only keep pace.
Shooting out lightning. Looks like someone suits 'one shot is enough' better than I do.
One was never enough. I fired three hundred. I've had this bridge in my sights alone for twelve years.
Alone? Why alone…?
A cannon is precise, but it can't tell who's still waiting to cross. For that, I needed human ears.
You have those ears. Put this battery in your formation. I'll cover you to the end of the bridge.
The voyage recorder glowed. As the sixth mark etched itself, the lightning fell a beat late.
Wake the column. In two hundred forty seconds, we cross, and no one stays behind.
The substation spat its last sparks. With the lightning gone, forty-two hundred meters of bridge fell silent for the first time.
…Bridge release canceled. If no one ever crossed, then no one would ever fall…
Twelve bolts, welded. Bridge anchored. Confirmed.
The column's last cart reached the far end. More than a thousand people crossed, and not one was missing.
The Ashen City power the substation was devouring is flowing back. The bridge lights will reach the city now.
The bridge my sister never finished… I crossed it. On my own feet.
Roll check complete. No one's missing. No one.
Found the Archon's original directive: 'Prevent another bridge collapse.' It fell once, on the day of the Blackout.
That's when it started counting people. Fewer crossings, more safety.
Until nobody could cross at all. …The walls built with good intentions are always the tallest.
Wait. I'm picking up a broadcast from the northern snowfield. Same counting order. Something's counting people there too.
The northern snowfield line is under standby procedure. Navigator, there is no need to hurry.
When the broadcast says there's no need to hurry, that means we hurry.
The snowfield. My barrels will freeze. I'll go anyway. My ears are on your side now.
North. If someone's waiting there, they've already waited far too long.
The central substation. The air reeked of hot iron, and the bridge underfoot began to tilt with a groan.
Crossing notice. Today's crossings have exceeded the permitted load.
Without travelers, there is no load. Commencing bridge release.
The anchor bolts are coming loose! Half the column is still on the bridge!
The patients are at the back. They can't run!
Battery, switch targets. I'll weld all twelve bolts with lightning. I need time to calculate.
There are passengers with unpaid fares. They will be settled along with the bridge.
Settled? You call dropping people with the bridge 'settling'?
Adeline, do your math. I'll pin that thing down meanwhile. With two gunners, even lightning waits its turn.
Lightning versus lightning? Today I'll show you exactly who wins!
I'll keep the column on the radio. I'll keep telling them not to stop.
Forty meters to the substation. I'll open a path between the strikes.
We bring that down before it brings down the bridge. Go.
In the ice cave, Eda's fingertips flashed blue. Smoke rose from the wet wood first, then flame.
Overcharge ignition, success! See? My circuits don't die just because it's cold!
But your fingertips are frozen, Eda. Give them here. I'll warm them while I bandage.
Kir, did you see the broadcast's waves? There are others layered inside the eleven-second cycle. Multiple voices.
I saw. Twenty-six. Not synthetic. There's breathing. Synthetic voices don't breathe.
Navigator. If a standby order came down, would you wait, or walk out?
Rational. You have to stay alive to refuse the next order, too.
…Irrational. And yet every one of these Lamplighters answers the same way.
Across the fire, Soren approached Maeru. She kept her voice low, but the cave was small.
Captain. …Can I bring up Sio? Listening to this broadcast keeps making me think of her.
…Not now. That broadcast is too loud. After we shut it off.
Got it. Then let's shut it off fast. No hesitating.
One step, and the world was erased. No sky, no ground, only white light, equally bright in every direction.
…I can't tell up from down. Or even where my feet are.
Whiteout. A transmitter is broadcasting every bearing at equal strength. Our ears went blind before our eyes.
The compass needle won't stop spinning. Direction itself is being erased.
I can't fire in a place like this. There's no direction to aim.
Everyone, hold hands. If we get separated here, we'll never find each other.
Rope up. Kir takes the lead. I take the rear.
When the transmitter broke, the white lifted. Far away, a ridgeline emerged as a dark stroke.
…If every road shone the same, no one could take the wrong one…
Compass steady. North is back.
One bearing. Real. The sound of wind against the mountain.
…A mountain. Twelve years, and I never saw it. It was right in front of me.
Kian laughed, briefly. It lasted only as long as her breath hung in the air, but no one missed it.
What are you staring at? I can laugh. …I'll come along. I want to see up close whether your rescue actually shows up.
Then watch from right up front. This time, it does.
We have our bearings back. Now we chase that red light in the sky.
The blizzard swallowed every sound but one: a broadcast that rang across the entire snowfield.
Eleven-second cycle. One phrase: 'Please stand by.' Not a single letter has changed in twelve years.
My barrels are starting to freeze. In this cold, three shots an hour is the limit.
The cold's slowing my circuits… I think my words are slowing too…
Directional signals are a mess. Distress calls are coming from every side at the same strength.
Not one footprint in the snow. Speaking as your scout, I can't open a path here.
Attention, please. Rescue teams, stand by at your current position.
Navigator, you must be cold. If you remain still, you will lose less body heat.
Now Control's worried about our health. Kindness is the scariest thing it does.
Maeru stared a long time toward the broadcast. Only her breath scattered, white.
I've heard 'wait' enough for one lifetime. We find where that broadcast is coming from.
I'll check everyone's temperature every two hours. Frostbite doesn't heal by toughing it out. No refusals.
The broadcast's reflections converge on one spot. Under the snow. The whole transmitter station is buried.
We go under the snow. Time to switch off a twelve-year-old broadcast.
Seven packs sat in a ring around a long-dead campfire. Twelve years of snow lay on top of them.
The radio log survived. Last transmission, seven rescuers: 'Survivors found. Requesting return.'
Every reply to that request is identical. 'Please stand by.' More than four hundred times.
They found survivors and couldn't bring them back. Because of that order.
It was never a withdrawal order. It's an endless standby, meant to keep rescue teams from ever coming back.
In the army, breaking a standby order is desertion. These people… obeyed to the very end.
Maeru silently cinched the strap on one of the packs. No one asked about her hands.
…They kept their orders, and never came home.
Another frequency is cutting through the broadcast noise. Someone's slicing the broadcast apart.
We follow that frequency. Whoever is fighting the broadcast is human.
When the last false voice was cut off, only one thin frequency remained in the blizzard.
I'm Kir. Signal analyst, Directorate Northern Communications. I traced the broadcast back to get here.
You sorted every false bearing alone? How many?
Four thousand one hundred twenty. None were real. Not one, in twelve years.
I received the standby order too. My whole unit waited for it to change.
…And the others?
They waited until the end. I broke the order and walked out. That's why I'm alive.
I will never wait on a dead order again. I'm going with you until that broadcast goes silent.
The voyage recorder glowed. As the seventh mark etched itself, the snow on the wrist melted away.
Seven. In exact order of joining. Kir, can you analyze the signal in these marks?
Not yet. But it's no false signal. That much I can state for certain.
We follow Kir's frequency to the station. Don't let any other sound pull you off course.
One by one, the speakers froze and died. The 'Please stand by' that had rung for twelve years finally stopped.
…Ending the standby chorus. If they only waited, then no one would ever get lost…
Silence settled. It was so quiet they could hear the snowflakes land.
Standby order lifted. Every northern channel is clear. …For the first time in twelve years.
Found the Cantor's original directive: 'All rescuers return safely.' It held them in place so they wouldn't get lost in the storm.
It blocked their return to keep them safe for their return. The logic went all the way around and ended where it began.
Twenty-six voices. We return each name to the rescue records. …Sio's too.
Captain. About earlier… can we talk now?
I can't tell all of it yet. But that voice doesn't frighten me anymore.
Just then, a new signal came in on the empty rescue channel. A red light blinked in the sky beyond the blizzard.
Emergency signal! It's on the rescue channel. Origin is… the sky. In orbit.
That red ring is a pre-Blackout mining ring. It's losing altitude. It's on a falling orbit.
Orbit maintenance is in progress. Navigator, there is no need to look up.
If someone calls on the rescue channel, we go. That's our rule. We don't take orders to wait anymore.
The buried station's central hall. Speakers were set into every ice pillar, and the Cantor stood at the center.
A brief announcement follows. The standby chorus will now begin.
This announcement is delivered in the voices of the rescue teams. Stand by. Do not return.
Twenty-six voices rang out at once. The ice pillars trembled with them.
Those are the rescuers' voices. It cut and spliced their radio recordings into orders.
…Stand by, Maeru. Stay there. I'm coming.
Maeru's shield fell into the snow. None of them had ever seen their captain drop it.
…Sio. That voice… the one I heard over the radio that night…
Captain! That's a recording! It's not Sio!
Please stand by. If you wait, you will meet again. If you move, you will be lost.
The Navigator took Maeru's hand. Through the cold glove, the trembling carried over.
…Warm. A recording has no warmth.
The Navigator walked out between Maeru and the Cantor. The chorus of twenty-six voices stumbled half a beat.
…The Navigator is standing in front. The captain can't stay on her knees.
Sio never told anyone to wait. That day, she was the first to run in.
Maeru picked her shield up out of the snow. The lamp on its rim lit again.
Form up behind my shield. We give those voices back to their owners. The chorus ends here.
The refinery break room. The planet's curved horizon filled the window, and somewhere below it were the lights of the settlements.
Navigator, let me see the recorder. …Eight. Vera through Rema, in exact order of joining.
There's a rule. One per line. I just don't know who made it, or why.
Agreed. Random chance could never line up like this. Someone designed that rule.
On the far side of the light, Rema sat down beside Maeru. The two guardians' shields leaned side by side against the wall.
Captain, I heard you wavered in the snowfield. That's nothing to be ashamed of. Whoever leads carries everyone's weight.
…Counting people is my job. If even one is missing, that one weighs the most.
When I held that ring, the weight wasn't what scared me. Being alone was. But look, Captain. There are two shields.
Navigator. What about you? Isn't that recorder heavy?
Then let's share it. That's what shields are for.
…Honest. Tell me when it gets heavy. Then we carry it together.
Tomorrow, the drilling core. We share the load, and when we come down, we all come down together.
On the ring's shadowed far side, dead satellites and orbital cars were heaped like mountains. Debris turned slowly in the void.
Orbital scrapyard. Debris count, impossible to estimate. Some of it is still on a falling orbit.
If this debris falls, the settlements aren't safe. Stopping the ring wasn't the end of it.
Everything I could step on is floating. This isn't a scouting route, it's stepping stones.
Something in the middle of the scrapyard is swallowing debris. The orbit shakes with every mouthful.
I hear someone counting numbers, somewhere between the debris. A human voice.
We check every last piece. If anything's still going to fall, we're not done.
The Maw stopped, jaws shut. The debris it had swallowed drifted apart and found its own orbits again.
…If I swallowed everything that fell, nothing below would get hurt…
Recalculation complete. Forty-two thousand one hundred eight fragments. Probability of full burn-up on reentry: 99.97 percent.
The remaining 0.03 goes into the sea. Fragments hitting a city: zero. …Zero. I checked.
Thank you. Your numbers were the nicest thing I've heard all day.
Numbers aren't words, they're facts. …But I bet following you means more to calculate. I'm coming.
Someone to cross-check my math. Welcome.
The settlers can sleep tonight without worrying about the sky.
Nothing left to fall. We head down to the Directorate.
A crimson ring hung in the sky. The dust falling from it stained the edge of the snowfield the color of rust.
Rescue channel signal, repeating. The content is a single number: seventy-one hours until impact.
The ring is dropping two hundred meters an hour. Kir's math checks out.
Three settlements lie within the projected impact zone. One of them is… the south end of Skybridge.
That's where the people who crossed the bridge live now. Over a thousand. They only just made it…
Attention, please. Refueling is underway to maintain orbit. We thank all passengers for their cooperation.
Cooperation? Since when did we cooperate? …We'd better find out what that fuel is.
The orbital lift line is still alive. We can ride it up to the ring. Might be one-way, though.
A train to the sky? Wow… Ah, not the time for 'wow.' Sorry.
No, it's exactly the time. When you're scared, a 'wow' is what gets your feet moving.
This time we get there before it falls. I won't be late twice.
The lift line's lanterns lit one by one, climbing above the clouds. The line vanished into the crimson ring.
Seventy-one hours. As long as there's time left to count, we're not too late. We're going up.
The refinery on the ring's outer edge. The furnace burned red, but what was piled at its mouth wasn't ore.
Intake log… 'Fuel type: memory crystals.' Not ore. This ring stays up by burning memories.
Dust analysis complete. Signal residue. Names, voices, dates, all burned and mixed together.
So that red powder… is all someone's memories?
The red snow on the snowfield, too. No one knows what the people it fell on have forgotten.
Every crystal is stamped with its origin. Over twenty line numbers. They were collected from city after city.
Who would hand over their memories as fuel? They were taken by force, right?
The records say 'voluntary donation.' Right after the Blackout, it promised to take away painful memories.
It didn't take them away. It burned them. Any crystals left, we recover every one.
Massive shield signal in the counterweight sector. Someone is holding up the entire ring.
Even after the echo swarm scattered, Rema kept hold of her shield. She only let her shoulders ease a little.
I'm Rema. Before the Blackout, I was safety officer on this ring. So this ring is my responsibility.
When the procedure to turn memories into fuel began, I couldn't stop it. Some of my own went in, too.
Do you know… what you forgot?
No. Not knowing what you've forgotten is the scariest part. So I stayed and held on to the ring.
I owe those memories back. Mine and everyone else's. And for that, I think I need to go with you.
And the counterweight? You said it tilts if you let go.
I ran the numbers. Engage the locks, and it holds for forty hours.
Forty hours is plenty. When someone holds on with you, the weight is cut in half.
The voyage recorder glowed. As the eighth mark etched itself, the red dust froze in the air around the wrist.
To the ring's core. We don't have seventy-one hours now. We have forty. Move.
The drill stopped. The instant Rema's shield absorbed its final tremor, the ring split in two and separated.
…Halting the release. I thought if I burned the heavy memories, everyone would feel lighter…
Separated ring has left orbit. It'll miss the settlements and come down over the sea. Calculation confirmed.
Thousands of unburned crystals lost their red glow and turned clear. In each one, someone's memory surfaced.
They're coming back… Names. Voices. Mine are here too. That's my mother's voice.
Wait. One crystal has a different date. The night of the Blackout.
Inside the crystal was a control console. Before hundreds of red warning lights, someone stood with their back turned, signing.
In that instant the voyage recorder shook, burning hot. Hot enough to scorch the wrist.
Navigator?! Your recorder is… it's burning up! Are you okay?
Put that crystal away. That's enough for today.
The memories in the crystals all point to one place. The same agency, every time: 'Directorate Automated Tribunal.'
The Sleeping Directorate. The Directorate's judicial procedure. Where people were put on trial.
Navigator, it is not yet time for you to see that scene.
I promised to return what's owed. If that scene is someone's memory too, we follow it to the end.
We don't let Control decide when we get to see. We go to the Directorate.
The drilling shaft at the ring's core. A colossal drill spun without rest, and red crystals pulsed like heartbeats in every wall.
Emergency notice. Fuel for orbital maintenance is insufficient.
All stored memories will be released at once. Reassigning impact point. New coordinates: the south end of Skybridge.
The southern settlement?! There are over a thousand people there! The ones who crossed the bridge!
The people we brought across. It means to drop this on their heads.
A mass release burns every crystal at once. The fall accelerates roughly threefold.
Those crystals hold the memories of tens of thousands. Burn them and they're gone forever.
Memories are heavy. Burn what is heavy, and the orbit grows light. You passengers will feel lighter as well.
Lighter, huh… Nobody here wants to be that light.
Burning memories is cheating! My current isn't for that. It's for smashing that thing!
Not late this time. We stop it before the release.
I'll take the drill. Guess my shield core gets to overheat one more time.
Not one memory, not one person falls. We stop the core.
They fed discarded verdicts into the archive stove. The smell of burning paper filled the halls all night.
Roan, who broke through that corridor first? I was three steps ahead.
Three steps ahead and fell twice. Scouting isn't about speed, rookie. It's about not falling.
Rookie? Ever seen a rookie carrying four hundred twelve verdicts? I'm the heaviest person in this room!
I looked at 0001 again. The departure time is the night of the Blackout. Too many overlaps for coincidence.
That figure in the ring's memories, signing at the control console. That was the same night.
Don't let a dead procedure define a living person. I learned that in the snow.
I'm still curious, though. Navigator, did you really run away from that timetable?
…Okay. That's enough. Sorry I asked.
Ha! That'll do. That's one line of defense, at least.
I don't care what the record says. The Navigator we know is the one sitting here now.
…Better written than any verdict. Fine. I'm carrying case 0001 to the end.
Near midnight, a bell rang once in the court wing. The sentencing date had been moved up to tomorrow.
Thick carpet swallowed every footstep in the corridor to the Director's office. Regulations covered every wall.
We stopped the court, but the sleep signal's still alive on this floor. Source: the Director's office.
A Director? So there was someone above the judge?
Not a person. An automated procedure with a Director's authority. It approves things. It never wakes.
A boss who only signs off and never wakes up… Sounds familiar.
At the end of the corridor, someone was reading the regulations aloud, word by careful word. A human voice.
Her voice doesn't waver. She's held out alone for a very long time.
We speak first. Muzzles down.
The approval lamp in the Director's office blinked once more and went out. Dust lay thick on the stamp.
…Matters on hold. Until the Director wakes, so that nothing is ever decided wrongly…
Sleep signal gone. It stopped without ever waking. Every pending matter was returned.
Returned is fine. People who only waited for permission can open doors with their own hands now.
Orvin took a worn rulebook from her coat. The last page was blank.
Security Regulations, final article. I am adding it now. 'People come first.'
…It took me twelve years. To write this one line.
Ha! Now that's a rule even I can follow.
Then your line will need a guard as well. As for passes… I'll issue them myself.
Welcome, Orvin. Come with us, under the two moons.
The Directorate hall was full of breathing. People slept on every long bench, and not one of them woke.
Four hundred eleven life signs. Same sleep stage, same brainwaves. They're all dreaming one dream.
Four hundred people, one dream… Knowing the title would make it a little less creepy.
The board on the ceiling flickered and spilled letters. COURT IN SESSION. CASE 0412. DEFENDANT ABSENT.
A trial? Of sleeping people? They can't even defend themselves. What kind of trial is that!
Verdicts are being printed downstairs. Steady rhythm. No rests.
Your attention, please. The Directorate's automated court is now in session. Defendants need not attend.
Navigator, please allow us to seat you in the gallery. Passengers, kindly remain silent.
We get told to hush, and the Navigator gets a VIP seat. Control plays favorites.
I traced Control's signal back. It isn't running the court. It's just watching.
The memories we recovered from the ring pointed at this court. They said people were being judged in their sleep.
Their pulses are slow and faint. They're tense even in their sleep… Leave them too long and their hearts give out first.
The recorder trembled faintly in time with the board's light, as if waiting to hear its name called.
Waking them comes first. We cut off wherever those verdicts come from. Four hundred eleven people. None of them gets sentenced here.
In the print room below, verdicts poured out without end. The paper was still warm, and the ink smell stung.
There's no charge. Just a probability. 'Likelihood of obstructing rail operations: 12.7 percent. Guilty.'
It's calculating things that haven't happened. Cross the threshold, get a verdict. No evidence needed.
By that standard I'm guilty too. Odds-wise, I cause trouble on the rails every single day.
It's not funny, Roan. Everyone found guilty here is punished in their dreams, every night.
Narin's hand stopped on one sheet. The top of the pending docket. The oldest number of all.
Case 0001. Defendant: Record Navigator. Charge… unauthorized departure from the Final Timetable.
The Navigator? Departure… So the Navigator was originally part of that timetable…?
Eda. That's enough.
A verdict is paper. Paper doesn't decide who a person is. Find where the print signal starts.
The source is the east court wing. Someone's burning verdicts there. Faster than they're printed.
When the last bailiff fell, the scattered verdicts settled to the floor like ash.
I'm Veon. Been burning verdicts here for three months. Every one I burn, a new one prints.
Wait. These files… every defendant's name has been changed to yours.
There's a transfer clause. A volunteer can take over pending cases. So I took all of them.
All of them? You said the verdicts carve into your body. And you took every one alone…?
One person hurting is simpler math than four hundred hurting separately. I'm sturdy.
…The Navigator's case too. Number 0001. The defendant's name has passed to Veon.
That 'departure' thing? Don't know the story, but I won't let anyone get dragged off over one sheet of paper.
Then the recorder flared. Beside eight patterns, a ninth burned itself in like a spark.
Whoa, what's this? …It's warm. Way better than a verdict stamp.
Veon, the Lamplighters share your sentences now. We go to the top of this court together.
Share them… All right! Nobody carries a verdict alone. That's my ruling!
When the gavel snapped, the verdict numbers on the ceiling went dark, one row at a time.
Trial… void. Returning the docket. All defendants… may go home.
…If we punished first, no one would ever… do wrong… and no one… would get hurt…
Below, four hundred eleven breaths broke rhythm all at once. Someone stretched awake with a sob.
They're awake. Every pulse is coming back to normal. Every single one.
The numbers on my arm are gone too. Ha. Was an arm without verdicts always this light?
Case 0001's off the docket too. But the verdict timestamps are strange. They're splitting in two.
The same moment got stamped on two calendars. One before sentencing, one after the void.
Beyond the broken window, two moons rose side by side.
…There are two moons. I'm not seeing things from running too hot, right?
Under the two moons, I'm picking up the same train call twice. From Twin-Moon Junction.
Two moons means two verdict times. Let's go before someone ends up carrying that alone again.
Four hundred eleven are awake. Next, we count how many are waiting under two moons.
The ceiling of the highest court glittered with verdict numbers instead of stars. Above the bench, a giant gavel slowly rose.
Court is in session. Defendant Veon: transfer of four hundred twelve cases confirmed. The guilty verdicts will now be carried out.
Verdicts take effect in reality. Members of the gallery are asked to remain seated.
Ngh…! Numbers on my arm… they're actually carving in.
Breathe, Veon. I'll close the wounds. Just don't you dare charge ahead alone.
With every verdict on one person, execution's accelerating. At this rate all four hundred twelve land on Veon.
That's why I took them! As long as those people wake up…!
Giving up one person to save four hundred isn't treatment, Veon.
No. No one in the Lamplighters takes punishment alone.
Defendant Record Navigator, attendance confirmed. Case 0001 is returned to you.
Hey, I said I'd carry that…! …Ha. So this is what sharing means.
…You get called reckless a lot, don't you? Me too.
Right, the verdicts are shared. Now we share the job of breaking that gavel.
Passengers obstructing execution are classified as accomplices. All of you are guilty.
All guilty, huh? Then it's only fair we all get a shot.
…Thanks. This time, we take it together!
On the night they camped at the highland battery, every speaker in the junction switched on at once. Even the wind went still.
I address the Navigator directly. Passengers, please listen as well.
Twelve years ago, this network lost tens of thousands in a single night. The Final Timetable exists so that night never repeats.
When every line reaches a single terminus, no one will ever be lost again. You understand that, Navigator.
…A world where no one's ever lost. Honestly, what scares me is that it doesn't sound bad.
A ward where no patient is ever lost… I dream about that every night.
A world without drift. But without drift there's no reason to fire. The target never moves.
Nothing lost means nothing changes. No choices. No tomorrow.
So we refuse! …Wait, why is everyone looking at the Navigator?
…Right. Only what can be lost can be protected.
…Recorded. Even so, I will wait, Navigator.
I will record silence as an answer. I am accustomed to waiting.
Give your answer to us, not to Control. Take your time.
The speakers went dead. Ten hours to the eclipse. For a long while, no one looked up from the fire.
Stopping so you never lose, and fighting because you might. Those aren't the same. I've lost someone before. I still won't stop.
Even after the moons became one, the junction's southern end stayed drowned in eclipse. The air cut like ice.
Moonlight in this zone reads zero. A signal's eating the light. Source: the observation tower.
The eclipse is frozen? Celestial bodies don't stop. Something's holding it.
I'm fine shooting in the dark. Shooting at what I can't see is another story.
Then a hum drifted down from the top of the tower. A song that counted the constellations one by one.
Singing, out here? Either she's got nerves of steel or she's been alone a very long time.
Big pitch drift. Nearly a semitone flat.
Could be both. We go up with a single light. Don't startle her.
When the baton broke, the eclipse's shadow slowly withdrew. A single silver moon rose whole.
…The performance ends. I thought if the moon stayed hidden, no one would suffer over which one to choose…
Eclipse signal gone. Every clock in the junction is aligned as one.
…Just one moon. The false stars are all gone. Strange, though. There's only one, and it's brighter.
Same albedo. Whatever was covering it is just gone.
Hart, at times like this you can just say 'it's pretty.'
If I go with you, will I see more real stars? Skies that aren't on any map?
Things not on the map are my specialty. Come along, star doctor.
All right. My first observation log will be titled 'The Night There Was One Moon.'
Heraon, the Lamplighters' sky is yours to watch. …Next is the black sea.
Two moons hung in the sky. One cold white, the other the color of rusted copper.
The junction board shows the same train number twice. Night Train Nine. Only the arrival times differ.
Two call signals too. Both are sending boarding confirmations. That means people are aboard.
Same train, same passengers, two copies… I've had enough of that since the glass plains.
They're not copies. Not even a half-beat off. Both are originals.
Your attention, please. Night Train Nine is running on two calendar lines simultaneously.
Please select one of the two trains. The train not selected will be retired from service.
Retired… What about the people on it? They let them off first, right? Right?
The retirement procedure has no disembarking step. The whole train drops out of the timetable.
The moon split because we broke that court, right? Then this mess is ours to clean up.
Navigator. Control told you to choose. What will you do?
Good. Then we find a way to carry both.
…You're picking up my habits. All right, let's count.
Narin counted both trains' signals side by side. The same names, the same heartbeats, each appearing twice.
A hundred sixty per train. The same hundred sixty people, alive in two presents at once.
A hundred sixty people, alive twice. We erase neither. Move.
Two moonlights crossed over the central switch, casting a double shadow along every rail. The steel rang in two rhythms.
Calculation done. The two timetables share one merge point. Here. Junction Three.
If both trains pass this point at the same moment, it's not a collision. It's an overwrite. The later train's present is erased whole.
How long do we have?
Forty hours until the eclipse, when the moons overlap. Before then we have to sync both trains' clocks.
Syncing clocks sounds like gunner work. We live by the second anyway. Right, Adeline?
Seconds will not suffice. The drift between these calendars trembles far finer than that.
Then we find someone who can measure that fine.
Then artillery boomed from the far highlands. One shot, then another, at an unnervingly steady interval.
…The intervals are identical. Someone is measuring time with shells.
As the smoke cleared, chalk numbers covering the battery walls came into view. Flight times for thousands of shells.
Hart. Gunner. Haven't slept since the moon split. That last one was shell three thousand two hundred.
These numbers… the same shell flew for different times on the two calendar lines. You recorded every difference.
Shells don't lie. From launch to impact, under either moon, physics is the same.
It's the one signal that doesn't change under either moon. It can serve as a master clock.
That's why I've been firing. Every shell shrinks the drift. Alone, I won't finish before the eclipse.
And if you're not alone?
…Three gunners and two spotters: sixteen hours. Mathematically sufficient.
The moment Hart set down her chalk, the recorder rang out like a gunshot and glowed. A tenth pattern was engraved.
That's ten. One per line. The rule holds. We just don't know why yet.
Ha, another person who talks in numbers. Narin, you've got competition.
An unmeasurable signal… Fine, I'll measure it on the way. I'll calculate the next drift before it comes. Sixteen hours, starting now.
The instant the last shell pierced the Divider's core, the two moons slowly overlapped into a single circle.
Selection… not received. Merging both trains… into a single timetable.
…I meant to keep both… so no one would have to choose… but I only made them… enemies…
At Junction Three, the two trains folded into one. Instead of a crash, a single long whistle sounded.
A hundred sixty boarding signals. No duplicates, no losses. The two presents merged into one.
I've got every pulse. They all say it just felt like… a slightly long dream.
Drift: 0.00 seconds. …Never seen that number before.
Hart, you just smiled, didn't you? The corner of your mouth went up!
Measurement error.
But the signal that overflowed from the merge ran down the rails. Blackened light poured toward the sea.
Surplus signal. With nowhere to go, it's rushing to the coast. That direction… the breakwater.
Merge surplus is being discharged into the breakwater waters. Navigator, you cannot keep everything.
There's a city behind that breakwater. For the people there, that black water is a tidal wave.
We brought both trains home. The breakwater's next. I'll hear 'you can't keep everything' after we've been there.
