Just before the eclipse, the two moons leaned toward each other over Junction Three. Two headlights approached from either side.
Master clock sync at 97 percent. Remaining drift, 0.02 seconds. One last shell will do it.
A correction. Both trains are genuine. Neither is a copy.
The unchosen train will be designated hostile. As no selection was made, both trains are designated hostile.
The roofs of both trains opened, and rusted gun barrels swung toward each other. The passengers inside slept on.
No, there are people on those trains! If they make them fire on each other…!
If the trains attack each other, the collision moves up. Eleven minutes until the eclipse.
Tell us to choose, then make both enemies when we don't? That's worse than the verdicts!
If choosing means abandoning, then we choose both.
'Both' is not a registered option. Input rejected.
If it's not registered, we register it. Soren, Adeline. On my signal.
Three gunners on one beat. This is going to look good.
Battery ready. Awaiting your order.
Three hundred twenty lives across both trains. Not one is an enemy. Our only target is the Divider. Fire!
By the stove in the breakwater post, the blue lantern burned all night. Maeru was the first to speak.
The night of the Blackout, Sio and I went to Platform Seven. To bring someone back.
…That's the story you said you'd tell 'later.'
The orders said only 'one rescue target.' The name field was blank from the start.
Sio went alone into the inner carriages to find the target. When the platform started collapsing, she radioed. She'd stay. She couldn't leave the target behind.
…Leaving behind someone who chooses to stay is part of rescue work too. The hardest part.
I led the wounded out first. On the train back, I left Sio's seat empty and fastened the belt for her.
I looked up that operation's records once. Only the rescue target is blank. Nothing on who erased it, or why.
Across the stove, a few glances quietly came to rest on the Navigator, then scattered.
The name was erased, but that night's coordinate remained. Where a coordinate remains, the story returns someday.
…All right. I'm counting on you, Navigator.
…If you find out, tell me first.
That's all of it. Tomorrow the tide will come for this lantern first. This time, I won't let go.
The sea beyond the breakwater was still black. Beneath the surface, something enormous breathed slowly.
Underwater contact. Over two hundred meters long. The surplus signal the Reaper gathered is still inside it.
The Guard called it the Blackwater. In twelve years it has never once surfaced.
Never surfaced means that when it has a reason, it'll come up all at once.
On a wrecked lifeboat in the distance, someone was hurling ropes and shouting.
That's a person! She's running a rescue out there alone, in those waves.
Her arms are rope-burned and bloody. She's been at this a long time.
Bring the boat alongside. We check on her before the Blackwater wakes.
The Blackwater exhaled one last time and sank. Hundreds of coordinates rose to the surface like stars.
…Storage terminated. I thought if I buried them deep, no one would drown searching for what they'd lost…
Tide signal zero. Wave height 0.2 meters. …First time I've seen numbers like that on this sea.
…The sea's quiet. It hasn't been this quiet in twelve years.
You saved more coordinates than I did today. I'll admit it.
Obviously. …But without your net I'd have lost half of them. I'll admit that much.
Let's treat those arms first. Three days without sleep, you said? You can rest now.
Sleep can wait! How much life-saving gear is on your boat? If it's short, I'll bring more.
…Get aboard, Mire. Our boat is always short of hands.
That night, for the first time, the sea reflected the moon without a ripple.
The waves pounding the breakwater weren't water. Clotted black signal gave off the smell of iron instead of salt.
Surplus signal from the twin moons. Water still rising. Behind the breakwater: one coastal city, twenty thousand survivors.
Something's floating in the waves. Glowing dots… buoys?
Not buoys. Coordinate signals. Thousands. One for every place a distress call went silent.
Abandoned routes are mixed in too. The forks we passed. The tracks we didn't take.
…There'll be coordinates of people who weren't saved, too. The places someone arrived too late.
Your attention, please. Lost items are drifting in the breakwater waters.
Missed passengers will not be recovered. Navigator, please do not look back.
Don't look back? If there are people behind you, of course you look back!
Leave them and they pile up. Rising 0.3 meters an hour. In three days it tops the wall.
Then what about those coordinates? We just leave them to the waves?
The twenty thousand in the city come first. We hold the wall, and pull the coordinates out one by one.
Even after saying it, Maeru couldn't take her eyes off the black water for a long moment.
Captain? …Let's go. Next wave's coming.
Before the second dike, one coordinate rose against the waves. Its call sign blinked faintly.
Reading call sign. Rescue Zero-Three… Identifier: Sio. Last position: Platform Seven.
Maeru stopped dead. The hand gripping her shield trembled once, visibly.
…Sio.
Captain… that name. The empty seat…
Timestamp: the night of the Blackout. …Twelve years without a single signal. And now, here, of all places.
The next wave caught the coordinate and began dragging it out toward open sea.
No. …I'm going!
Captain, stop! Jump in there and you'll be swept away before the coordinate is!
The current's flowing to the north dike. There's a live shield-net signal there. The coordinate could get caught.
…North. Hurry. Please.
As the echoforms fell back, the coordinates in the net swayed like fireflies. The surf quieted by a beat.
I am Orsa, the last shield of the Breakwater Guard. For twelve years I've fished coordinates out with this net.
A recovered coordinate must be anchored to the present. Otherwise the next tide takes it again.
Orsa pressed one coordinate gently with the edge of her shield. Rescue Zero-Three. The trembling light went still and solid.
It's anchored. This coordinate lives in today now. It will not drift back to that night again.
…Could someone lend me a lantern?
Maeru opened an empty lantern and moved the coordinate inside with both hands. The lantern lit, small and blue.
…It's blue, but somehow it looks warm.
Twelve years. …Thank you, Orsa.
In that moment the recorder swelled with light like a rising tide. An eleventh pattern was engraved in the shape of a wave.
I will see every drifting coordinate home, to the very end. This lantern included.
Massive reading at the center of the tide. Something's devouring coordinates, and it's targeting the anchored ones first.
When the sickle broke and fell into the sea, the black tide sank as if holding its breath.
Harvest… halted. Returning… lost items.
…So no one would have to see what they left behind… if I gathered it all under the waves… no one would look back… and cry…
One by one, the coordinates in the net regained their light. Beyond the wall, windows lit up across the city.
Water falling. No breach in the wall. Zero damage to the city.
Some three thousand four hundred coordinates recovered, all anchored to today. I'll open their routes home one by one.
Captain, your lantern looks brighter than before.
…Yes. A little.
Then a rusted key drifted in on the calm water. The name engraved on its bow had been scraped away.
There's signal left in the teeth. Cathedral door standard. It points inland, somewhere with no name on the map.
I hear singing from that direction. A hymn. Its lyrics are… empty.
The next section is the Nameless Cathedral. Please have your names ready upon entry.
Have our names ready? Like an admission ticket? I don't like that.
Everyone hold tight to your own name and follow me. …To the Nameless Cathedral.
At the heart of the breakwater, the black tide rose like a pillar. At its tip hung a colossal sickle-shaped engine.
This is the lost-and-found office. The recovery period for drifting coordinates has ended.
Anchored coordinates will now be harvested. A past clinging to the present obstructs navigation.
The coordinates in my net are being pulled away. The anchored ones first… it's using them as bait.
At Maeru's hip, the blue lantern tilted toward the tide as if being pulled.
…Sio's coordinate too.
Pull still rising. Every sweep of that sickle raises the water at the wall by half a meter.
Please choose. Release the coordinates, and the breakwater holds. Keep them, and the city drowns.
Choose again?! We already saw that trick at the twin moons!
…This time, I'll answer.
I won't let go of the lantern or the wall. Twelve years ago I left someone behind. Never again.
Good. I take the wall, Orsa takes the net. Captain, you just hold on tight to that lantern.
Two shields against one wave. That's enough.
And three guns against one sickle. Math done.
In the sacristy beneath the cathedral, everyone sat around a single candle. The hymn seeped faintly through the walls.
Let me sum up. Different lines, independent signatures, twenty. We have twelve. Eight to go.
If a new timetable can be written, the current one can be discarded. Control's Final Timetable included.
Is that why Control recognized the Navigator from the start? Because it knew whose wrist the recorder was on?
…But who made this rule? The number twenty, the condition of independence. Someone designed this.
Without thinking, everyone looked up at the speaker in the ceiling. Control, always so quick to cut in, said nothing this time.
Silence is a signal too. If Control won't answer, it doesn't want to.
Or it hasn't finished calculating. Either way, that's its problem.
Whoever made the rule, every signature was someone's own choice. From Vera to Tiel. That's not a rule. That's people.
Navigator, don't those signatures weigh on you?
…A good answer. Your pulse didn't waver.
Ha, already on to the next count? Fine. Eight. I'll open the way.
That's enough for tonight. Tomorrow, the altar. …Before you sleep, call the name of the one beside you.
In the ossuary beneath the cathedral, the hymn never stopped. Nameless plaques crowded every cold stone wall.
The Choir Lock is down here. It's where the cathedral locked away the oldest names it collected.
The seal signal's still alive. Even with the Prelate stopped, the names down here haven't been released.
If they're the oldest names, they've waited the longest too.
Someone stood at the ossuary entrance, leaning on a sword. She didn't turn even as footsteps approached.
…She knows we're coming. But she hasn't said a word.
That's a pilgrim guard's stance. A sword that watches over holy ground. We mustn't cross it lightly.
Not drawing her sword is an answer in itself. We approach slowly.
With the sound of the Choir Lock cracking, the song fell silent. Letters rose, one by one, on every plaque in the ossuary.
…The hymn is concluded. I believed that kept within the song, no name would ever fade…
The names are going home. One, then another… Pulses outside are answering.
Seven hundred ten names unsealed. The oldest predates the Blackout.
Raen sheathed her sword and knelt on one knee before a single plaque.
…My fellow pilgrims. Now I can call them by name.
…So you stood here alone all this time to guard those names.
…Nothing left to guard. May I follow you?
You said a blade can't lie. Yours already answered. Let's go, Raen.
Behind the departing Lamplighters, the names going home echoed like quiet footsteps.
Hundreds of names were carved above the cathedral door. Each time one was read aloud, its letters fell away like ash.
The teeth fit. It's the key from the tide. We can open the door.
Then let's open it. This name here is… huh? What did I just read?
Roan, the name you read just vanished from the door. And from your memory.
Your attention, please. Welcome to the Nameless Cathedral.
Names will be collected as seal maintenance fees. Navigator, you are exempt.
Exempt? Just the Navigator? Is this some VIP treatment again?
A levy means it's spent maintaining something. We must first learn what this cathedral is sealing.
The hymn has no lyrics. Only blanks where names should go. Our names are meant to fill them.
Then we just don't say names? Eda, Eda, Eda… Phew, still there.
Spend names sparingly. Keep calls short. If someone answers, that's your confirmation.
The door opened. At the end of a long nave, thousands of candles burned on the altar in place of names.
If it's one name per candle, over three thousand people have been taxed.
Three thousand names. We give them all back. …We're going in.
A levy ledger hung on every pillar of the nave. Beside each name, instead of a date, was stamped 'PAID IN FULL.'
This isn't a list of the dead. Every one of them is alive. This cathedral taxes the names of the living.
What happens to the people whose names are taken?
They live. It's just that no one can call them anymore. Not their family. Not even themselves.
That's terrifying. Um, the… the one with the cannon… uh, her name is…
…Soren. It's me. It's okay, Eda. Your name came to me a beat late just now too.
Wait, that one with the shield… we met at the dike… Damn it. It's right on the tip of my tongue.
Orsa. I'll tell you as many times as it takes. If you forget, I'll simply say it again.
The levy is speeding up. Call each other's names and listen for answers. If that stops, we stop.
There's a pulse-like signal from the choir stalls. Steady. A signal that beats without a name.
As the choir scattered, thirty-two rhythms carried on quietly beneath Tiel's fingertips.
I'm Tiel. I was this cathedral's medic. I've remembered each person who lost their name by their pulse.
Tiel pointed to the stone tablet behind the altar. Among the erased names, a single sentence remained whole.
The final verse of this liturgy. 'When twenty independent signatures from different lines are gathered, a new timetable may be written.'
Signatures… one per line. The patterns on the Navigator's recorder. Eleven so far, and the rule has never once broken.
So without knowing it, we've been collecting the right to write something new?
In that moment the recorder throbbed like a pulse. In time with Tiel's rhythm, a twelfth pattern was engraved.
…It beats exactly with my rhythm. A mark that remains in place of a name. Far kinder than this cathedral.
Until every name returns, I will remember your pulses.
A new timetable… A page we write ourselves instead of a verdict? I like it!
The levy signal beyond the altar just spiked. The cathedral's noticed us.
The priest's mask cracked and fell. Behind it, instead of a face, was a single blank name tag.
Collection… halted. Returning… seal maintenance fees.
…Without names, no one would ever be forgotten… If there were no names to call at all… no one would ever feel… they'd lost…
The three thousand candles on the altar flickered all at once. Each flame lifted a single name and flew out of the cathedral.
Pulses and names are locking back together. Thirty-two… no, all three thousand.
…Maeru. Captain of the Lamplighters. Sio's lantern is still lit. Everything's where it belongs.
Captain, don't you ever lose your name again! I'm going to call it a hundred times a day!
…Ten times a day will do.
Wait. Some of the names that flew off are drifting south. Toward the desert.
The signal's drawing tracks on the sand. Tracks that aren't on any map. With a timetable attached.
A timetable for a train that doesn't exist. It's filling its passenger list with the stolen names.
If names are drifting with nowhere to return to, then they're coordinates I must recover as well.
Verdicts, twin moons, tides, a cathedral… and now sand? Fine. Bring it all on!
Twelve of twenty. And not a single name left behind. …We head for the desert.
Atop the altar, a towering masked priest-engine swung its censer. Wherever the smoke touched, letters melted away.
Payment notice. Seal maintenance funds are insufficient. Designating a high-value contributor.
Lamplighter Captain Maeru. That name is hereby collected.
The censer smoke wrapped around Maeru. And from every mouth, one name slipped away without a sound.
Captain! …Captain, your name… what was it? I knew it a second ago.
No, no… I call that name every day. Why won't it come…!
…I am… the Lamplighters'… I am…
Her pulse is unchanged. The heart remembers. But someone has to call her name.
Only the recorder still shone with letters that hadn't gone out. In the exempt record, the name remained.
As the Navigator called the name, Tiel tapped out a rhythm. Once, twice, at the pace of a heartbeat.
Now. Everyone, call it with this rhythm.
The recorder's light etched the name into the air. Tiel tapped a rhythm to match the letters.
We can read it. Everyone, call it to this rhythm.
Ma… Maeru. Captain Maeru!
Maeru. …Right, Maeru! Who could forget our captain's name!
…I hear it. Maeru. That's my name.
Requests to cancel collection are not accepted. Commencing re-collection.
Take it as many times as you like. There are people here who'll call it back every time. …Everyone, names confirmed. Let's go!
The desert night carried sound far. From the shade of a ruined relay post, the crackle of the fire rolled past the dunes.
Eda, is that circuit of yours only good for lighting fires? You were half a beat late every fight.
Because you kept cutting in front of me! Want me to shock you too next time?
…Try it. But hit me properly. A half-hearted zap is more annoying.
Ha. Being a courier wouldn't have been bad… but I'd never have had a night this loud.
…Navigator, let me see the recorder. Something showed when the thirteenth was carved.
At the very bottom, a scratch older than Vera's signature. Not a line pattern. …It looks like handwriting.
All right. I won't write guesses. Only what I can confirm.
…You can cover it if you want. Just don't carry it alone.
Why the long faces? Aren't you the ones taking down a stationmaster tomorrow?
We are! Shocking Rias comes after that!
Bank the fire. We leave for the station at the dunes' edge at first light.
Hold out the recorder and ask her to look into it
Cover the mark with a sleeve
At noon the mirage zone rippled like water. On the horizon, one train became three, then four.
Interval between trains: 4.2 seconds. The same consist is being copied on a delay.
Every bearing is false. There's only one real whistle. I'll pick it out.
Ghost trains, and now mirages? Does this desert know anything but lies?
The more lies around, the more honest the shot has to be. Just hit the real engine.
Manifest fragments keep leaking from the engine's signal. Passengers the stationmaster never boarded are still out here.
One line of footprints in the sand. Mirages don't leave footprints…
If there are passengers left, we go. Mirage or not, even for one.
As the mirage lifted, the heat settled. Only real footprints remained in the sand.
…If it arrived nowhere… no one would ever be late…
…First time I've seen it. Tracks that prove you arrived. Mirages never leave any.
Hey, courier. In the life I didn't choose, I was someone like you. She looked awfully carefree.
Carefree? A courier? You know nothing. …I'm Zern. I needed a crew to run with. Count me in.
Welcome. We may be slow, but every one of us arrives.
So you admit you're slow. Zern, the lead spot's mine.
Every rail trace bends upward. Toward the capital. If we're late, it closes.
Late? I hate that word. Let's go!
The sand stayed warm long after dark. From beyond dunes without a single rail, a whistle arrived first.
No wheel ruts, no sleepers, and a train is running anyway. What do I even put in the scouting report?
Write 'does not exist.' No mass, only signal. Twelve cars in the consist.
I've caught the passenger manifest. Two thousand four hundred. …Every name recovered from the cathedral.
Names freed from the cathedral. They should have gone home to their owners. Why are they on that train…
A silhouette sat at every window. None looked out, and none got off.
Attention, please. Lives you did not choose are also in service. Please board the car of your choice.
The car of my choice… why does that sound so tempting?
The more tempting the announcement, the steeper the fare. Has that speaker ever given anything away?
They just got their names back and got dragged off again? Whose verdict was it this time?
Not a verdict. A timetable. A route that doesn't exist is laid across this entire desert.
A stop line was drawn in the sand. It bore an arrival mark, but no wheel tracks led away.
Next scheduled stop: the northern dunes. If the train stops there, passengers can get off.
Two thousand four hundred. We leave no name at those windows. North.
When the train stopped, familiar faces surfaced in every window. Through the blowing sand, they smiled without a care.
…That's me. Courier bag, no Lamplighter badge. She looks so relaxed.
Third window: me, in a lab coat. If I'd accepted the offer to stay that year. The odds favored her.
The manifest is shifting. The longer someone stares at a window, the harder their name sets into a passenger slot.
Only the window before the Navigator stood empty. Not even a grain of sand showed in the glass.
Same as on the glass plain. A person whose record is locked reflects nowhere.
You have no unchosen life, Navigator. You chose everything already, that night.
Don't listen. That broadcast pretends to answer and leaves only questions.
…Right. I'll stop looking. Honestly, I was a little jealous of her.
Eyes off the windows. The manifest signal comes from the front of the train. That's where we cut it.
As the phantom passengers scattered, the sand began to cool. A thin thread of smoke rose from Rias's muzzle.
See? They stand on the side you didn't choose and beckon. Follow them, and you're done.
The manifest lock is broken. But as long as the train runs, the names will set again.
So leave a mark. The last choice each of you actually made. That's your anchor.
Last choice, huh… Deciding to come here this morning. Does that count?
…That was quick. It counts. Doesn't have to be grand. Just real.
Going back to Platform Seven after twelve years. That's my mark.
The moment Rias scored her own mark into the sand, the recorder flared hot. The thirteenth pattern.
…What's this? What did I just do?
A line signature. Thirteen of twenty. Your choice was carved in as this line's ending.
Choices aren't recovered. They're made new. …Fine, I'll come. Fall behind and I leave you.
The timetable bears a stationmaster's seal. The station at the edge of the dunes. That's the root.
When the last car broke away, the station clock stopped for the first time. Long shadows scattered across the sand.
…Attention, please. This station is now… ending service.
…Even the lives you couldn't choose… I only wanted to give them one ride…
The names on the manifest are scattering. Back to their owners this time. The heartbeats are returning, one by one.
…Stupid stationmaster. If you wanted to give rides, you should've carried the living.
Still, I think I understand the wish. To have someone remember the roads not taken.
All two thousand six hundred names have found their receivers. Not one is left on the manifest.
Then the rails beneath them shook off the sand and rose. The steel curled into the sky and vanished into the clouds.
The rails lead upward. Coordinates… the capital loop. But its orientation is inverted.
A road that falls into the sky. I hope it's a weight a shield can bear.
The capital will soon terminate its connection to all outside lines.
You, however, may enter at any time, Navigator. Headquarters is waiting.
One invitation, a whole crew. Guess we're crashing together.
The desert's done. The capital's next. We count there too, one person at a time.
The station at the edge of the dunes had no walls. Only pillars, a clock, and an endless string of cars stood on the sand.
Welcome to Dune Station. This station is the terminus for lives not chosen.
The cars are multiplying. Manifest at two thousand four hundred… no, it just hit two thousand six hundred.
The greater the regret, the stronger the car. Your regrets make excellent fuel.
Burning regret for fuel? Disgusting. I'm uncoupling every one of those cars.
A car slid in among them. In its window, the Roan who never joined the Lamplighters waved.
Roan, get away from that car. The manifest signal is winding toward you.
Passenger Roan, would you care to transfer to the courier service? In that life, you lost no one.
…Tempting. But these people aren't there. I'll pass.
Good choice, Roan. A life with something to protect weighs more than a life with nothing lost.
Aim for the couplings. One car at a time. One person at a time.
The coupling intervals are uniform. Three seconds per car and it's cut.
Three seconds is too long. Run!
They hung a lantern in a concourse set right side up again. Outside, the lights of still-inverted streets hung like stars.
The court had you for unauthorized departure, and now final signing authority. Navigator, the charges are piling up!
Veon, you're grinning while you say that?
Of course I'm grinning. I took that case under my name. More charges just means more for me to carry.
But aren't you curious? Authority used once. I'd stay up all night pulling that apart.
Deleted records leave recovery traces. Given time, I can verify it.
Dig up the past later. Look at which way you're walking now.
I look at the present, not the records. …But this is the Navigator's call.
Understood. I'll save the coordinates of the deletion traces. Whatever turns up, we read it together.
Good. That's right. The past isn't going anywhere.
…You're a seriously weird team. Nobody suspects anybody. It's like a bug.
Not a bug. A rule. Tomorrow, the central level, where the Auditor waits.
I want to know the truth
For now, we move forward
The palace district was still upside down. Chandeliers sprouted from the floor, and staircases descended into the sky.
My hacks don't work here. What's holding gravity isn't a device. It's that crown.
So the crown is holding up the city. That must be heavy. Heavier still after so long.
Artillery in an upside-down palace. If the shells fall upward, that's not on me.
I'll handle the ballistic correction. Just tell me which way is falling.
One faint signal under the palace. Encrypted. …Someone's watching us through a screen.
If they're only watching, they have their reasons. We go down and ask. Without scaring them.
The sound of the crown cracking rang through the whole city. One by one, the inverted floors returned to their places.
…If there were no outside… no one would ever fall…
…The floor numbers match. Basement twelve is below ground again. After twelve years…
You held out well. May I ask your name?
Soa. …I've never talked with people this long without a screen.
Soa, you built that firewall solo, right? With two hackers, we'd be unbeatable.
…Can I come with you? Not from behind a screen. Beside you.
Of course. Behind a screen or beside us, we count everyone.
Found a shipping log in the palace records. Seed crates, addressed to the Garden of Zero Signal.
Seeds? The capital was sending flowers? …That feels ominous.
The capital's sky lay beneath their feet. Shattered towers fell soundlessly toward the clouds.
First time I've seen a building fall up. …Wait, are we the ones upside down?
Both. Gravity points a different way in every district. 'Down' changes every three steps.
So one misstep and you fall into the sky. Simple. Don't misstep.
There's a train running upside down through the clouds! There are people in it, right?
Capital population on record: thirty thousand. Living signals: half that. Scattered across the loop's twelve stations.
Attention, please. The capital is now permanently isolated from all outside lines. Passengers, remain where you are.
Permanent isolation? Locking up an entire city without so much as a verdict?
The isolation order originates at the city's center. Directorate Headquarters.
…Headquarters. Where every procedure began.
A single line of light ran straight through the middle of the inverted sky. Every distant rail bent toward it.
That line isn't on any route map. But the signal of every line leans toward it.
Beautiful. Though anything that straight has usually been pulled taut by force.
Catch the falling first. We dig up what that line is at Headquarters.
On the station wall leading to Headquarters, a protocol was carved upside down. Its letters dripped toward the ceiling.
Emergency Protocol Zero. 'Isolate the capital from all loss outside.' Not an accident. An order.
The inversion isn't a side effect of the isolation. It is the isolation. It erased the very direction called 'out.'
No way out means no way in for rescuers. Like me, twelve years ago. They'd arrive too late.
Building fall rate rising three meters a minute. In six hours, even the lowest levels drop into the sky.
Navigator, Headquarters remembers you. The main gate is always open to you.
The main gate's open? That's practically advertising a trap.
They're only letting the Navigator in. What are we, luggage?
One signal near a side door. Someone in the middle of the inversion zone keeps opening and shutting it.
We don't use the main gate. We cross the falling districts to that side door. Within six hours.
Perin tapped in the last command, and every 'down' in the district aligned. Drifting dust settled on the floor.
Ta-da. Everyone's different 'down,' bound to one reference plane. Just this district, though.
You turned the inversion controls against themselves? Without calculating?
The devices do the math. I just lie to them. 'This is down.'
At that moment the recorder lit up. A fourteenth pattern surfaced on the wrist, sharp and clear.
Huh? My hack on your wrist? …No. That's not something I did. That's something I chose.
Fourteen of twenty. Welcome, Perin.
With the plane aligned, a Headquarters terminal woke. An old authority register scrolled across the screen.
Admin list. Director, control chief, track supervisor… huh, what's this at the top?
'Record Navigator: final signing authority.' Authority exercised: once. Details deleted.
…Turn it off. The people falling come first.
When the scale broke, the falling buildings stopped. Dust drifted slowly down, in the right direction.
…Audit concluded. The load… cannot be measured.
…If no one ever came back… nothing would ever collapse…
No one returning, nothing collapsing. Not wrong math. Just not math anyone can live with.
All capital districts normal. Isolation lifted. Fifteen thousand living signals reconnected to the outside lines.
Fifteen thousand people can send word outside now, right? Wow, my voltage is spiking!
Every terminal in Headquarters lit at once. The original path of the isolation protocol streaked across the screens.
The original source isn't here. The Garden of Zero Signal. The capital's protocol was a copy.
The original isn't preparing isolation. It's preparing a reset. Its target… the memory of every line.
Beyond the righted sky, the line of light had grown sharper. Now even the desert rails reached it.
The terminal has a name for that line. 'The Last Line.' A plan to bind every route into a single terminus.
Navigator, the garden's flowers will bloom soon. A world without pain is near.
A memory reset? My least favorite command. No system gets to choose a person's direction. I'll wreck it all the way.
We don't need a peace bought by forgetting. To the garden.
The central audit chamber was a colossal scale. On one pan sat the capital; on the other, nothing at all.
The audit begins. The capital's load will now be measured. Please do not move.
Those readings are wrong. It isn't weighing buildings. It's assigning load to each life sign.
The will to return is judged an overload. The wish to go home is what collapses the structure.
The wish to go home is an overload? Some people held on for twelve years on that wish alone.
Oh, I get the scale's logic. No one wanting to leave means the city never shakes. Worst bug ever.
The Record Navigator is excluded from measurement. Authority holders are not subject to audit.
…Special treatment again? Creepily polite.
The isolation protocol is locked into the scale's axle. Break it and the whole capital gets its reference plane back.
No need to weigh us. Every one of us has somewhere to return to.
Then we're heavy people. Good. Let's go in heavy!
Overload? Great! Pile my weight on too!
The scale tipped. The whole capital rang out once, deep and loud.
They built a fire in a maintenance tunnel the flowers couldn't reach. Only where the scent ended could everyone breathe properly.
I used to be a garden porter. Hauled seed crates, drew water. Nothing special, right?
Nothing special? No one carrying seeds means no flowers!
…Huh. You're the first to put it that way.
…Mind if I confess something too? What I saw in the flowers.
An old station canteen. Sio was sitting next to Maeru, laughing.
…Soren.
I knew Sio too. Not for long. I didn't realize I still remembered that laugh.
…Next time. Not 'later' this time. 'Next time.'
Thanks, Navigator. Words come easier by a warm fire.
…I remember that laugh too. Brighter than any lantern.
Good memories are too precious for bait. I'm not giving any away tomorrow. Not even to the gardener.
Ask to hear more about Sio
Tend the fire in silence
The air in the greenhouse was heavy. Drops beaded on the glass roof hung in midair, never falling.
Time runs at a third of outside speed. One hour here is three hours out there.
Never been in the greenhouse either. Porters weren't allowed this far.
Deeper in, a single flower keeps blooming and wilting. Like a pulse.
That's the Zero Bloom's core. Even with the gardener down, if that survives it'll sprout again.
There's an herbal smell in the air. Someone's been growing something in here.
We check it down to the roots. Time runs slow here, so we run fast.
When the last petal fell, the suspended drops came down all at once. Slow time fell like rain.
…If only we went back to the start… a world where no one had lost anything…
…Oh my, rain. In all the time Bael's been here, it's never rained.
The Zero Bloom's withered. Now the garden's just a garden.
Then I'll take just one seed. To plant somewhere it can bloom again, in time that flows properly.
Good idea. Let's plant it together at the next camp.
Come with us, Bael. We're always short on herbalists.
Hehe, all right. Just match my pace, slowly.
Artillery signals from east and west. The civil war has begun.
…Then 'slowly' will have to wait. Let's go.
Every season's scent rose at once in the garden. Spring blossoms, summer grass, and first snow, all from a single field.
…Everyone's pulse is slowing. The tension is draining away far too fast.
I feel it too. Warm, like right before sleep. …Places like this are the most dangerous.
The whole garden is one server. Every flower stores a memory fragment. How many… I can't even count.
Attention, please. Remain in your happiest moment. There is no need to go further.
'No need to go further' is the most suspicious line yet. Everyone who stopped for it is right over there.
People sat all through the flowers. Every one smiled with open eyes, and none of them stood.
…They're smiling, but nobody answers. Quieter than echoforms.
Breathing and pulse are normal. No injuries. But I can't tell how many years they've sat like that.
By signal count, seven thousand. Including people brought here from the capital.
Reset preparation signal from the core. When the bloom completes, every line's memory will be overwritten by this one field.
It's warm and nice… but for some reason I can't make a fist.
Let's not step on the flowers. Somebody's best day is inside each one.
Seven thousand. We get every one of them up. Happiness is given back to the waking, not the sleeping.
The deeper they went into the field, the thicker the scent. With every step, their footsteps sounded farther away.
…Oh, it's the base with the lights on. Everyone's laughing, and I can smell warm soup…
Eda, that's not real! …Wait, what's happening to me? It's the day someone called my name out loud…
Snap out of it. The flowers don't erase memory. They keep only your safest moment and close every other road.
Right now we're each standing in our safest place. That's why none of us can walk forward.
The flower before the Navigator showed only one scene. A stalled carriage, a quiet seat, eyelids closing.
I remember the moment you were most at peace, Navigator. That seat, as you closed your eyes.
…Platform Seven. That was the most peaceful place? That's where we lost someone.
Eyes off the flowers. Navigator, Eda, Veon. Follow my voice.
…There's a path of withered flowers farther in. Someone cut it on purpose.
When the garden keepers fell, the flowers around them bowed their heads as one. The sweet scent thinned for a moment.
Phew, done. I liked watching you fight. The way you trust each other with your backs.
Have you been alone all this time? In this garden?
Yeah. Everyone sat down by the flowers. My sister too. She cries when I wake her, so I couldn't.
But I'd rather be with you, in a tomorrow I don't know, than in a comfortable past. Can I come?
While Karn waited for an answer, the recorder answered first. The fifteenth pattern.
Ooh, the recorder answered first. Says you passed.
…Passed? That was a test? Didn't know. Glad, though.
Fifteen of twenty. Five signatures left.
The path Karn cut runs all the way to the core. The gardener is at its end.
We'll wake your sister together on the way back. That's a promise.
As the closed flower withered, the garden's scent drained away all at once. Across the field, people began to rise.
…Concluding… maintenance procedure. Opening… the repository.
…I only wished… to let you stay somewhere… it didn't hurt…
Look, my sister's getting up. She's crying. …But she's walking out.
Crying is fine. Walking out is what matters. I'll check her pulse.
All seven thousand conscious. No memory loss.
Then the roots at the garden's core flared red. The reset authority's signal split in two and raced toward both horizons.
Hey, the authority's running! Sent east and west at the same time!
Receivers: the queens of the Eastern and Western Lines. If either approves, the other's evacuation route is scrapped for good.
Succession claims from two lines have been received simultaneously. Please await the result.
…It means civil war. It won't be long before the guns can be heard from here.
I said an unknown tomorrow over a comfortable past. …So let's go protect that tomorrow first.
An entire evacuation route could vanish. We go and stop it. We save both.
At the garden's core, one enormous flower stood closed. Around it, translucent petals floated like shields.
Welcome to the garden. This is the repository of your happiest moments.
Those petals… they're my memory. The base with the lights on. Everyone's laughing.
Mine's there too. The canteen. …Sio, too.
Every attack shatters a memory. Will you break your most precious moments with your own hands?
…I've already given one away. It hurt. But I could see ahead.
Memories don't live only in petals. They stay in the pulse, in the fingertips. Shattered, they still beat again.
Back down from something hiding behind memories, and the memories become hostages.
Navigator, your seat has been kept empty. You may rest there again whenever you wish.
That seat stays empty, and we move on. The Navigator is here, with us.
…Sorry, Sio. This time I'm looking ahead instead of at your laugh.
Me too! We can light the base up again. As many times as it takes!
Aim for the stems between the petals. Whatever memories break, we build again when we're home.
Behind the field hospital, four medics sat around a fire steeped in the smell of antiseptic.
Noar, how many did you see today? I had twenty-one.
Thirty-four. …I don't like counting, but if I don't, I forget.
I know. I counted to the end of the evacuation line too. So I wouldn't forget.
Write the pulse beside each number. Then the numbers stay people.
At the edge of the firelight, Eda sat hugging her knees. Her circuit glowed dimmer than usual.
…Honestly, I'm scared. Echoforms are fine, but people shooting people… it's so scary.
I'm glad someone's scared. War makes people forget that first.
Eda, it's okay to say you're scared. The one who says it out loud is the bravest.
…Heh, it's warm next to you, Navigator. Feels like I'm charging a little.
Sixteen… every one a person. With this many of us, it's okay to be scared.
Tomorrow… I'll go scared. But I'll still go.
Sit beside Eda
Show her the patterns on the recorder
The throne car circled the loop line without stopping. Even after the crown was dismantled, as if awaiting someone's command.
It's unmanned. But its batteries are aimed at both capitals at once.
…There's someone in the next car. One pulse. Very steady, unwavering.
A throne without a crown. Let's go see who's guarding it.
Sometimes a throne is better left empty. Let's go teach it that.
Reload cycle: twelve minutes. Nine minutes to the next shot.
Nine minutes is enough. Not one shell lands on either capital.
One by one, the Sovereign Engine's barrels sank. At the end of the line, the throne car finally stopped.
…If only there were orders… no one would ever lose their way…
That night, a long table was set in the junction's waiting hall. The two queens sat at its eastern and western ends.
…Western Queen. By the rites, the guest raises her cup first.
Don't know the rites, Eastern Queen. But bread gets split in half. You know that much?
…We know it. Even our forebears' rites wrote down that much.
The name's Teran. …Two crowns at one table. No order ever showed me that.
I'm no one's knight anymore. But if another wrong order comes, I'll refuse it at your side.
That's enough. Welcome, Teran.
Soldiers from both sides are asleep in the same tent. No need to count tonight. Everyone came back.
Gunsmoke hung over the junction where the two lines met. Gold banners flew over the eastern rails, red cloth over the western.
Hear us, people of the Eastern Line. The lawful heir to the Directorate's charter is the Eastern Line alone.
The seal and the rites our forebears left us are the proof. We shall protect all through order.
Charter, sure. Western Line, listen up. Paper doesn't fill stomachs.
We've got thirty-eight thousand mouths. The crown goes to whoever feeds them. Done.
One talks like an old decree, the other like a market stall. Both equally loud.
Both batteries are sighted across the junction. One shot and the fighting starts.
Refugee signals: forty thousand on the east side. Seventy-eight thousand in all, stuck at the junction.
Attention, please. The victorious line will merge all lines. Passengers, please await the outcome.
Merge? So the winner swallows everything. What kind of succession is that?
The authority that flew out of the garden came here. If those crowns get hold of it…
The winner can erase the loser's evacuation route. Permanently.
So whoever wins, tens of thousands on the other side lose their way.
Crowns aren't our business. People are. We save both sides.
Inside the captured signal house, succession papers printed without pause. The paper never stopped, but there was only one signature line.
These aren't succession papers. They're merger orders. One signature from the victor binds every evacuation route into a single track.
Every line into one? I've seen this structure… It's identical to the line of light over the capital.
…It's the Last Line in miniature. Every route into a single terminus. This war is a rehearsal.
Do the two queens fight knowing this, or not knowing?
I'd bet not knowing. If they knew, both would've lowered their guns.
Navigator, the rehearsal proceeds smoothly. One signature is enough. You remember that, don't you?
…That broadcast keeps talking only to the Navigator. It's creepy.
If their world ends with one signature, we gather twenty. That's our answer.
One field hospital signal. Wounded from both sides tied to one channel. Someone linked them on purpose.
When the lancers withdrew, only the smell of antiseptic remained in the tent. A single lantern lit forty-two cots.
I linked the medical signal into one. When one side hurts, the other hears it too.
A way of sharing pulses. It resembles my rhythm records. Far gentler, though.
It isn't gentle. Once you can hear it, it just gets harder to shoot.
…The guns on the front have thinned. That signal must have reached the trenches.
Then the recorder glowed quietly. Without a sound, the sixteenth pattern was carved.
…Is this a signature? I haven't promised anything.
You already did. You counted forty-two as one.
Then I'll keep the record. Not who won, but who came back.
Sixteen of twenty. …That mark beneath the first pattern looks sharper today.
The lancers fell back toward the junction. First, we secure the evacuation route for the wounded.
When the lance broke, the gunsmoke over the junction lifted. Gold banners and red cloth stirred in the same wind.
…Suspending… the succession procedure.
…If all were one… there would never again be anything to fight over…
So even the crown wanted peace. Only its method was wrong.
Peace? Peace from erasing one side is just a graveyard.
You are the Navigator, we are told. To which of the two lines would you give the crown?
Ha. Nobody needs it, huh. …Can't argue with that today.
Wear it together? That answer is not in the rites. …But we shall write it down.
An old succession seal rolled out of the broken crown. A set of coordinates was engraved on its back.
Coordinates decoded. The Archive of Afterglow. The true succession record is kept there.
The Archive… where our forebears were said to have sealed away 'the original of that night.'
Original or whatever, bring it. If it says who signed first that night, we'll know who started all this.
At those words, the old mark beneath the recorder's first pattern flickered once, cold.
The Archive of Afterglow will soon put its records in order. Navigator, there is no need to hurry. The ending is already written.
…We go to the Archive. Whatever is written there, we read it together.
No one needs the crown
Wear it together
At the heart of the junction, the two queens stood on the same platform for the first time. Between them, a machine with a silver lance descended.
My soldiers in the trenches heard the east groaning and wept. Can't shoot like this.
We received the same report. It is not in the rites, but we shall permit the guns to rest a while.
Warning. Truce is treason. The succession procedure requires a single victor.
The medical signal is classified as an attack on command. Eliminate its source.
…It means me. It's all right. I set the signal to hold even if I'm cut off.
We won't let you be cut off. Noar is one of us.
Lamplighters? …Hey. That tin can with the spear, whose side is it on?
The crown's. Not ours, nor the Western Queen's. …Only now do we see it.
Both sovereigns, please stand back. The lance will not stop until a victor is decided.
A victor? Nobody needs one. I'm snapping that lance first.
You two, stay back. We'll hold here.
…Ha, giving me orders? Fine. Just for today.
Impertinent, but right. Eastern guard, stand down.
Under the camp lantern, Seb opened the tablet from the original stacks. The turning pages fell silent, and a time from the night of the Blackout surfaced.
I'll read it exactly as written. '23:52. Final Timetable draft, first signature. Signatory: Record Navigator.'
The recorder shook, burning hot. Now everyone knew whose back it had been, signing before the control console.
'00:51. The draft halts not only the lines, but people's choices. Irreversible.'
'The Navigator erases their own memory and is sealed at Platform Seven. Condition for scrapping: twenty signatures from different lines.'
The last line was handwritten. 'Let the next Navigator choose again.'
There's one appendix. A record of a rescuer who guarded the sealed seat to the end. …Name: Sio.
Only the sound of the burning wick remained. No one spoke first.
…I once asked who made this rule. So one person's signature can't be overturned by one person alone. The answer was right here.
So you're the one Sio guarded to the end. …So. What will you choose this time?
Good. From where you stopped twelve years ago, this time we go together.
I took over that case, remember? Here's my verdict. Not guilty! And everyone here is an accomplice!
Accepted. That settles it. We leave twelve years ago where it is.
Tell Sio too. …Though she'd have laughed before you finished. That's who she was.
Choosing is yours. Holding the line is ours. …Tomorrow, I count everyone again.
Deep in the stacks, each sheet of parchment was written over a hundred times. New letters kept growing over the scraped-away ones.
This is the palimpsest layer. The names everyone thought were erased are all pressed underneath. Thousands of them.
The layers are offset by half a beat each. The deeper, the more genuine. Overwrites always pile up on top.
Then we go all the way down. If there are people pinned under there without their names.
Beyond the parchment heaps, a gun sight flashed. Someone was still standing watch at this depth.
A live battery in an archive? Didn't expect guards. Guess we should say hello.
The aim keeps tracking us. Echoforms can't hold aim this long. It's a person.
Weapons down. We don't fire first.
When the Palimpsest Core stopped, the layered parchment peeled away sheet by sheet. The ink at the bottom shone as if freshly written.
Names. People overwritten out of existence since the Blackout. Three thousand… no, over four thousand.
Like drifting coordinates. Abandoned, but never gone. We'll send every one of them home.
'The unrecorded die twice.' An old saying. …Today, no one died a second time.
My watch is over. The shelves I guarded are gone, so now I'll guard the people outside them.
You're bringing the whole battery? That's a heavy load.
'What is heavy endures.' This one's a real quote. Source: the plaque over the archive gate.
The restored names became motes of light and drifted up through the vents in the ceiling, each on its way back to its own line.
The names are on their way. So are we. The Last Line won't wait for us.
Pages turned without pause on shelves that climbed to the ceiling. The Archive of Afterglow was rewriting history even now.
The titles on the spines change every three seconds. It's not the same book. A different past keeps getting shelved in the same slot.
The broken crown's coordinates pointed here. So the real succession record is somewhere inside.
The record of how the war stopped is already fading. The wounded are still exactly where they were.
Wait, our names were in this book… just a second ago? Now it's blank!
Then the old speakers between the shelves chimed the same note at once.
Attention, please. This archive is currently organizing intervention records.
Your footsteps, passengers, are unnecessary footnotes to history. They will be deleted shortly.
Your record alone, Navigator, will remain untouched. Regulations require that originals be preserved.
'Original,' huh. That voice gets oddly tender whenever the Navigator comes up.
Original? Then the Navigator's case file I took over must be in here too. I'm reading it first!
People before books. We secure our own records before they're erased.
…Navigator, check the recorder. Are all sixteen signatures still there?
The sixteen marks had not faded. In the whole archive, theirs was the only light that could not be erased.
Then that recorder is our reference point. We head deeper in, where the deletion signal is strongest.
The expedition log on the reading desk turned its own pages, bleaching white line by line. What it erased were the Lamplighters' names.
The first page is empty. The dead line, the rescue signal, the day I joined. All of it is becoming something that never happened.
It's not just the paper. Your name just came out of my mouth a beat late.
It's erasing us in the order we joined. At this rate, all sixteen of us are blanks within six hours.
Once the records go, we'll be strangers to each other. Along with every reason we fought together.
The heart remembers. But when the paper forgets first, the mind follows.
Delete commands always leave logs. If I trace it back… huh? Someone's writing it all back in.
One signal at the center of the stacks. It's writing faster than the archive can erase. It's a person.
Through the sound of erasure came a voice, murmuring without pause.
If it's a person, we bring her back. Before our names fade out.
As the echoforms scattered, the words running down Seb's arm went still. Contradicting sentences rested side by side on one body.
See? Everything the archive erased is right here. It can't delete any of it while I'm alive.
Store contradictions in one body and the archive can't pin down what to delete. Logically sound. Physically reckless.
Totally reckless! So let me come with you. Even a living index lasts longer with people beside her.
The recorder lit up. As the seventeenth mark surfaced, the faded names in the expedition log returned to their places.
Seventeen. Three to go. This number weighs more than any shell count.
About that recorder. There's exactly one matching mark on the archive's lowest floor. In the original stacks from the night of the Blackout.
Opening it needed an index, and now you have one. Me. …But once you read it, there's no going back to not knowing.
…That's fine. We only ever go forward anyway!
…We open it at camp. With everyone there.
The Index Predator's catalog collapsed, and torn cards fell like snow. On every scrap, a name bled back into view.
…I tried to erase every meeting. If none of it had ever happened, no one would grieve…
The crew called each other's names, once each. Not one answer came late.
Every pulse is normal. Everyone remembers everyone. …Thank goodness. Really.
Hold on. At the very bottom of the layers the Predator swallowed, one document survived.
'Last Line opening order. Execution: 00:00 tomorrow.' …This isn't a record. It's a scheduled command.
Meaning you can delete the record, but the command stays. Burn the whole archive and the opening still won't stop.
We don't wait on dead orders. We cut them first. That's all.
Then every speaker in the stacks came on, softly.
Navigator, you have confirmed the truth. In twelve years, the draft has not been wrong by a single line.
Please conclude what you began. One final signature, and no one will ever be lost again.
Nobody's concluding anything! The Navigator is writing something new with us now!
I'll pin that scheduled order in my index. Proof that it's a fixed command, not a prophecy. And I'm coming along.
One day left. We head for the Last Line. We get there before it opens.
At the heart of the stacks, a colossal card catalog yawned open. Every card that spilled out held one member's joining record.
Reading room patrons, please be advised. Index cleanup is beginning. Duplicate, contradictory and intervening entries will be discarded.
Passengers whose joining records are discarded, please treat one another as strangers.
With every torn card, a stranger's wariness spread through the crew's eyes.
…Who are you people? Whose signal is this?
No idea. Funny thing, though. You're strangers, but I feel like I could trust you with my back.
The cards can tear, but the index is right here! Vera, the dead line. You came to give the rescue signal back to people!
…Right. To give the signal back. Those words are mine.
So we're strangers. So what? We choose each other again from scratch. We've done it once. Second time's faster.
Warning. Bonds without records are not approved. Please submit your reason for traveling together.
We heard the whole truth at camp. After that, no one left their seat. That's our reason.
Submitted. Every one of us standing here is the reason.
Great, we'll do the index cleanup for you. I'm taking point!
The night they first slowed the clock, camp lanterns stretched along the rails. One by one, the crew came to find the Navigator.
Navigator, I'll hold tomorrow's signal to the end. Even if your recorder goes dark, I'll find you.
Get some sleep. Medic's orders. …Honestly, I'm scared too. So let's both close our eyes a while.
Weight is meant to be shared. The night you signed alone is over.
Keeping this short. …You've fought well so far. Do the same tomorrow.
I'm no good with words. I'll just be next to you. That's enough, right?
Everything said tonight is in my index. Whatever gets erased tomorrow, it stays here.
Navigator! Remember I said war scares me? This time it doesn't. …Well, half of me isn't scared!
Last of all, Maeru climbed into a carriage beside the tracks and tugged each seatbelt, one by one.
…Lot more seats to check this time.
…Thanks. You take this row, I'll take that one. Leave the one empty seat as it is.
It's Sio's. It stays empty for now. When the day comes to bring her along, I'll fill it.
Tomorrow we fight to buy a day. I won't let a single seat go empty. …Except that one.
Behind Midnight Terminus, construction was still underway. Driverless rail carts hauled sleepers over half-laid track without rest.
Zero construction error. None of the tremor you'd find in track laid by people.
So it's a worksite with nobody on it. Nobody to yell at us if we smash it!
…No. There's one track-cutting signal. Someone inside is undoing the construction.
The sound of cutting steel rang out steadily in the distance. The cutting was just a little slower than the laying.
If someone's cutting that alone, we help. So the faster side wins.
There's a supervisor's signature in the construction log. And every date is written backward.
We follow the sound. We reach it before the machines do.
Midnight Terminus's great clock stopped at 11:59. The second hand trembled but never moved to the next mark.
Locked one minute short of opening. This station can never be a terminus now.
…Best station I ever designed. A terminus no one ever arrives at.
I laid the tracks. Now I'll lay tracks that take people home. From your side.
Good. Laying suits you better than cutting.
Pointless talk. …Thanks.
Cut pieces of track piled up beneath the stopped clock. The station was left with an hour that ended no one.
I'm naming this time in my index. 'The Minute That Ends No One.'
One minute left standing is enough. Let's go spend the rest of our day.
Outside the archive, new rails glowed from one horizon to the other. Every line curved toward a single point.
The Last Line. Twenty-four hours until opening. The pull of the rails tilted the lanterns of distant cities all one way.
The Ashen City, the Sky Bridge, the snowfields, the capital… Every city we've passed through is being dragged to the same coordinates.
It matches the archive's scheduled order to the second. Midnight sharp. No delays, no early start.
Then, as if the whole sky had become a speaker, the announcement came down from every direction at once.
Attention, all passengers. The Last Line opens tonight at midnight.
All passengers, please board. This train stops at every station, and you may alight at none.
Navigator, a reserved seat awaits you. The same one as twelve years ago.
That seat? The one at Platform Seven? Ugh, I've got static all over!
They're pulling the refugees in too. Thousands of them are in no shape to resist on their own.
One day. Within one day, we must protect every one of these coordinates.
One day… plenty for scouting, tight for fighting.
We hit the nearest relay first. …Navigator, don't lose sight of that recorder's light.
The Lamplighters began walking against the tilt of the lanterns.
The relay's giant reference clock didn't tick; it thrummed, low, like a heartbeat. Every city's clock turned to its rhythm.
Can't delete the opening order from here. The core is deeper in. But guess what I found?
This clock is the reference time. Every line checks it to decide when midnight is. Slow it down, and midnight comes late.
How much can we slow it? Numbers, not guesses.
If we keep cutting the reference signal, up to twenty-four hours. Exactly one day.
A day is enough to reach the Last Line's core. We can't cancel it, but we can get there.
If you can't delete the order, cut its clock. Rational.
Problem is who guards that clock while we cut. Control won't just sit there.
I'll put this day in my index too. Not a day we were given—a day we earned.
We buy a day. We pay for it ourselves. On to the next relay tower.
As the last signaler fell, white steam rose from Yurien's barrel. The reference clock's pulse slowed once more.
Thanks. Alone, ninety seconds was never enough. Tonight, for the first time, I had time to spare.
Yurien. Long-range gunner. Since the day they started laying this line, I've been delaying construction one day at a time with shells.
Using shell flight time as a clock? …Same as my method. Margin of error?
Point-two seconds per shell. A little tighter than yours.
…Point-four was a long time ago.
The recorder etched its eighteenth light, the same pattern as the impact tallies carved on Yurien's barrel.
I'll spend my remaining shells buying time. Down to the very last one. That's my signature.
Eighteen! Just two left. I've never been so happy to see empty slots.
We see this day through. The signalers' main force is in front of Midnight Terminus.
The tower collapsed, and the compressed day scattered. The red lights died, and the reference clock's slow pulse returned.
…If you know when it ends, even fear can be counted. With the end set in advance, no one would feel uneasy…
Reference time locked! The opening moves from tonight to tomorrow midnight. We actually bought a day!
Four shells left. Four shells for a day—not a bad trade.
Amid the cheering, Maeru raised the radio. The retreat team had missed their scheduled report by an hour.
Retreat team, respond. Vera, Iri, Liv, Orsa.
Instead of an answer, a static-laced rescue signal came back. The same sentence, repeating at the same interval.
Retreat team here. The tracks… only lead back to the start. I've lost count of the laps.
No one's hurt. But every lap, someone forgets something.
Coordinates confirmed. The whole retreat route has closed into a loop. A track with no end—the Unfading Circuit.
Passengers in the Circuit section, please wait in accordance with return procedures.
Navigator, you have bought a day. I will be watching to see whom you bring back with it.
So the day we earned goes to four people. …No—of course it does.
People before the opening. We go to the Circuit. We bring all four back.
A colossal signal tower stood in the plaza before Midnight Terminus. The lights at its crown went dark red one by one, like a second hand.
That's the Doom Signaler. Every hour we delayed is stockpiled inside it.
Delay notice. A delay has occurred in the operating timetable.
The delayed time will now be returned. Commencing midnight barrage. Passengers, please lower your heads.
It's packing a whole day into one shell and sending it back. If it lands, every hour we bought is gone.
The refugee column is inside the blast radius! Thousands are still on the tracks!
Vera, Iri, Liv, Orsa. You're the retreat team. Open a way out for the column.
I'm done arriving late. This time I'll go ahead and wait for you.
The rest of us bend the trajectory. With four gunners, even a day-sized shell can be made to miss.
I'll run the numbers. Yurien, I'm trusting your point-two.
Warning. A timetable without a fixed end causes passengers anxiety. Midnight must be kept.
Anxious nights are when gunners get busiest. Tonight we only need to bend one trajectory.
All right—gunners take the sky, everyone else the tower! I'll open the way!
The retreat team's lanterns receded toward the column. Only one red light remained on the tower.
They set the camp lanterns in a ring at the heart of the Circuit, and Moen closed her notebook. This time, each would speak in her own voice.
To give the rescue signals back to people. That's not a reason one lap can erase.
Even late, I deliver to the end. I said it myself this time, so I won't forget.
Toa, Seon, Adeline, Kir, Tiel… With every reason spoken, the Circuit's rails slowed a little more.
So no one carries a verdict alone! However many laps, that doesn't change!
I buy time down to the last shell. …Saying it out loud is a little embarrassing.
To be a witness to choices. …But just now, someone other than us answered.
On the Circuit's deepest track, a faint lantern flickered. The lantern Maeru had carried trembled in the same rhythm.
…Platform Seven rescue team, Sio here. At the sealed seat, still holding. Maeru, can you hear me?
I think this is as far as I go. It's not your fault. When they wake up, tell them: choose together this time.
…Did you hear, Sio? A promise. This time, we choose together.
…Thank you, Sio—from the one you protected. Twelve years late, but in person.
For twelve years, I never cleared your seat. …I'm not waiting anymore. I'm taking you with me.
When the record ended, the lantern on the deep track shone long once, then went out. In Maeru's arms, the other lantern grew warm.
At the seam where the Circuit's rails met, the grinding of steel rang without end. It was the sound of the loop holding itself together.
The seam widens by a hundredth of a millimeter every lap. This is the weakest point.
Then there's no reason to save shells. Just give me coordinates.
Wait. Life sign near the seam. The same person pops out at the same spot every lap.
Someone tumbled out of the gap, gasping, then was dragged back into the loop. Thirty seconds later, the same spot, again.
She's hurt. The same wound every time. When she comes out next, we have to catch her.
Catching is my specialty. Need fast hands? Call me.
We catch her next lap. Set up in front of the seam.
When the Ouroboros Rail snapped at its seam, the steel that had been a loop stretched out long. For the first time, the track had a front and a back.
Loop signature gone. This track only runs one way now.
…It's not pulling me back. Thirty seconds passed, and I'm not back at the start.
You're all right now. Breathe slowly. This is a road you only walk once.
Then… what's next? Where do we go next? I can't remember the last time I said 'next.'
Next is wherever we're headed. If you want to come, there's a seat for you.
I'm coming. Anywhere, as long as I don't have to count.
Light from a distant lantern spilled in from the end of the straightened track. Velk stared at it for a long time.
I'll write it down. Velk, her first 'next.' Dated today.
At the mouth of the Circuit, the same milepost repeated without end. Every sign read: '0 km to the start.'
The whole track is a single loop. Forty kilometers around, no exits. Exactly one hour per lap.
A road where running forward gets you back to the start. So much for my pride as a scout.
We bought a day, and this is where it goes. …That's fine. Time spent on people is the most precious kind.
Four sets of footprints were stamped on the track dozens of layers deep. The same steps, treading the same spots again and again.
The retreat team's footprints. Counting the layers… that's thirty-one laps.
…We bring all four back. We leave no one.
Then the same announcement rang from every station in the Circuit, each a half-beat off the last.
Attention, please. The Circuit section is currently undergoing return procedures.
Return requires one substitute passenger. If one of you remains, the rest may go home.
Designating a substitute passenger. Navigator, will you choose the passenger again this time?
Hear that, Control? The answer is 'no one.' We don't buy cheap deals.
Footsteps instead of words. …Good. That's the clearest answer there is.
There's no loop that can't be broken. Heavy as it is, let's go in.
The thirty-second lap, we run together. Moving in.
On the thirty-second lap, the Lamplighters found the retreat team. The four sat in a circle on the tracks, watching one another.
You came… Thank goodness. No one's hurt. But something's wrong.
Why did I join the Lamplighters? I remember holding the floodgate. After that… it's blank.
Last lap it was Orsa. One person per lap loses their reason for joining.
Whoever loses their reason is designated the substitute passenger. They have no reason to stay, and none to leave.
The ticket core is at the center of the Circuit. It erases reasons to make someone 'fine to leave behind.'
Liv, it's in my index! The flooded signal station: 'Even a late rescue gets delivered to the end.' Your words!
…Even a late rescue. Yes. That's my voice, all right.
But the core erases faster than the index can record. Next lap, it'll be one of us.
Then we reach the center this lap. Retreat team with us. Nobody falls behind.
As the echoforms withdrew, Moen opened her worn notebook. Every reason erased over thirty-two laps was written there in dense pencil.
I'm Moen. I kept records at the Circuit's signal box. I've written down the reasons of everyone who circles here—by hand, not by machine.
There's one way to get a reason back: say it again in your own voice. I'll read you what I wrote.
I take responsibility for bringing drifting coordinates home. …Hearing it in my own voice, it has weight again.
Handwritten records… as an archivist, I'm a little jealous. …Let's write together, Moen.
The nineteenth light etched itself into the recorder—thin as a pencil stroke, and impossible to erase.
I'll come with you. At the last moment, you'll need someone to witness who chose what.
Nineteen. One left. …First time my hand has shaken while counting.
One left. And before that, we lose no one here. On to the core.
As the ticket tore, the Circuit's track revealed an end for the first time. Beyond the broken loop, a straight road stretched away.
Default changed. 'Sacrifice procedure' deleted. 'Everyone returns' entered. …Written by hand. This is the original now.
…An empty train can bring no one home. I believed someone had to stay for the rest to return…
No one stayed behind. Maeru called the names one by one, and every name answered.
Every drifting coordinate has come home. Retreat team, return complete.
Everyone's pulse is normal. …It took a while, but no one's missing.
Then, beyond the broken Circuit, beams of light rose across the world. The lanterns of all nineteen lines they had crossed flowed in one direction.
I traced the flow back. There's one convergence point. The place the Directorate's blueprints call 'the Last Lantern.'
Same as the terminus coordinates in the archive's scheduled order. At the end of the Last Line stood the Last Lantern.
Navigator, the light of every line is gathering. Preparations are nearly complete.
I will wait for you before the Last Lantern. Just one signature, as twelve years ago.
I'll watch the final moment. Who chose what—I'll write it to the end.
We go to the Last Lantern. …And Sio's lantern rides with us.
Above the gates of the Circuit's central station floated one enormous ticket. Crew names surfaced on it and vanished, one after another.
Passengers of the return train, please be advised. Verifying departure conditions. One substitute passenger is required.
The sacrifice procedure is the default for return. If just one of you remains, everyone else may go home.
That again. Drop one, save the rest. Easy math, wrong answer.
If someone has to stay, I'll stay. …That's exactly what it wants us to say. Not falling for it.
I've been writing down the ticket's code. 'Sacrifice' isn't an order. It's a factory default.
A default? Defaults exist to be changed! Where's the settings menu?
You lack authority to change settings. The default exists to protect you, passengers.
The authority is right here. No one who circled this loop ever chose to stay. I saw every one of them.
The Lamplighters leave no one behind. That's our default.
One ticket makes a fine target. Nobody rides in anyone's place.
I'll punch that ticket! With lightning, full of holes!
The names on the ticket began to spin faster. It was the sound of choosing the next name to erase.
The last camp. The five founding members sat in a circle around one small lantern.
Remember? The first lantern we lit. We cranked a hand generator all night just to light one section.
Four of us cried when that one section lit up. Everyone but Maeru. Though she had her back turned, so who knows.
Three, precisely. I had dust in my eye. …According to the record.
And I came up with the name! The ones who open the lantern road—the Lamplighters! My head was totally overcharged that day!
After that, we grew. Twenty-four now. But the very first one we brought in—I never said it properly.
All five turned to the Navigator at once. The small lantern's light spread evenly among the six of them.
Navigator. It's late, but I'll say it properly. …Welcome to the Lamplighters.
No need. I've had your front since the first scouting run. Always will.
Whoa, hands in! Can I send a spark through? Just once!
…Don't.
…I'm logging it. As of today, the Lamplighters have six founding members.
Great. Then tomorrow the six of us go light a lamp. We just need to bring in that twentieth signature.
Tomorrow will be long. …Sleep well, all of you.
Beneath the Last Lantern, a vertical shaft plunged out of sight. A dropped flare fell and fell without reaching the bottom.
The Lumen Abyss. Where erased records sink. Thousands of names are layered in the signal from the bottom.
The walls of the abyss bore the marks of every line the Lamplighters had crossed, carved upside down.
Names overwritten in the archive, reasons erased in the Circuit… It all flowed down here in the end.
We cannot leave what drifts behind. We go down.
I'll hold the rope. So the way back never breaks.
Deep places are scary, but my light can reach the bottom!
Going down. Coming up, we'll be as heavy as the names we bring.
As the floor of the Lumen Abyss brightened, the sunken names rose as motes of light. Thousands of them climbed back up the shaft.
They won't all fit in my index! …That's okay. From now on, these names will be remembered on their own.
I watched every name rise. Not one missed.
Everyone safe, all the way up the rope. The way back held.
Some days later, Platform Seven. The first train of the new timetable waited to depart.
So where's our first stop? This is the first time we get to decide.
Vote's unanimous: 'Anywhere, all together.' …That's not a destination.
Maeru checked the seatbelt of one empty seat, then set a small lantern down in it.
Sio. This time, we go together.
Window seat. Perfect for the view.
…Move out.
At the end of the world stood a single lantern. Its glass, as large as a rail carriage, was empty; in twelve years it had never held a flame.
Before it, the light of nineteen lines poured in like rivers—from the rescue signal on a dead line to the pencil strokes of the Circuit.
The Last Lantern. The Last Line's terminus and the first station of every line. On the blueprints, they're the same spot.
The ignition mechanism is sealed. Twenty layers of locks. Force it, and the whole lantern shatters.
The day we bought is down to a few hours. And the opening is still scheduled.
The lantern's glass trembled. Every speaker on the Last Line switched on at once, like a single indrawn breath.
Navigator, I have been waiting for your final signature.
For twelve years I have not deviated from the draft by a single line. It is exactly as you wrote it.
Please conclude it now. Then no one will ever lose anything, ever again.
But then nobody can go anywhere! That's just… stopping!
Conclude? Don't make me laugh. We've only just started.
I'll write it down. Before the Last Lantern: twenty-four arrived. Not one missing.
We open the seal first. We'll prove this isn't the end—it's the first station.
When the recorder touched the first seal plate, nineteen lights rose across the glass in turn. Only the twentieth slot stayed dark.
The seal doesn't count heads. It counts independent signatures from different lines. Twenty. We have nineteen.
We've got way more than twenty people. Can't the five of us each sign one?
No. You five share one line. The seal spots a copy of the same record in half a beat.
Then the twentieth has to come from a line nobody has tied off yet. There's exactly one left in my index.
The Final Line. The defensive line guarding the Last Lantern. Its defense signal is still alive.
Navigator, there is no need for a twentieth. Your signature alone is sufficient.
That voice has gotten impatient. Twelve years of waiting, and it can't manage half a day.
We go to the Final Line. The twentieth isn't someone we bring—it's someone who chooses for herself.
The twentieth slot was still dark. Beyond it, from the Final Line, a single defense signal blinked as steadily as a sentry's steps.
As the echoform tide receded, Lavent lowered her shield. Every defense signal linked to it fell quiet at once.
Lavent. The last of the Final Line garrison. For twelve years, I guarded the lantern from behind this wall.
My job was to guard it until someone came to light it. …You came. So now we light it together. My signature too.
The recorder trembled. The moment the twentieth light rose, all twenty marks joined into a single ring.
Twenty! My index is full. This one recorder weighs more than the entire archive.
Twenty independent signatures from different lines, confirmed. …The math is done. What's left isn't math.
Attention, please. Line signatures cannot replace the draft. …They must not be able to.
That voice just wavered. I'm writing it down. Terminus Control, first hesitation.
Twenty, gathered. …Navigator, it's your turn.
I'll be the wall all the way to the lantern. Don't worry about your back. Just walk.
The floodgate fell, and darkness surged in. The Lamplighters did not hold it back. With twenty lights, they drew a road through it.
…I locked the light away so no one would wander in the dark. Without darkness, no one would ever lose their way…
The Last Lantern caught fire. The darkness did not vanish. But wherever anyone stood, the way home could be seen.
…New timetable confirmed. First coordinates: twenty signatures from different lines.
Passengers, please… choose your own destinations. Navigator, have a good journey.
Hear that? From every line, it's not rescue signals coming in—just hellos. Thank you, Navigator.
You did well. Sleep deep tonight. This time it's a real medic's order.
Case closed! Toss the file in the campfire. One more light tonight!
I'm leaving the last line of my index blank. The next story starts there.
I saw it. I saw you choose. I wrote it all down.
Guess you won't need a wall anymore. I'll keep watching your back anyway.
Sio would've laughed. Me, of all people—'one shot is enough'—needing twenty.
Navigator! Where to now? Anywhere's fine—I'm fully charged!
Record complete. …No. Record begins. Day one of the new timetable.
I'll open the next road too. Wherever it leads this time.
…All present.
Before the Last Lantern, a colossal floodgate barred the tracks. In the dark beyond it, countless things were breathing.
Attention, please. This is the Final Line floodgate. Ignition of the lantern is not permitted.
Light the lantern, and every darkness gains a route as well. Wherever light reaches, darkness follows.
Therefore, ignition will be turned against itself. The moment it lights, every line will be shut inside this gate.
For twelve years, I guarded this wall alongside that gate. Same purpose. Wrong method, that's all.
Then the speakers above the floodgate came on, softly. The voice was quieter and kinder than ever.
Navigator. That night twelve years ago, you signed to protect everyone.
I have never once forgotten that intent. You may rest now. I will protect the rest.
…Navigator. If you go with that voice, I won't hold it against you. But you choose. With your own hand, this time.
The Navigator signed not the draft but a blank timetable, and the recorder's twenty lights gathered around the signature.
That's not a signature on the draft. It's the first line of a new timetable. …Same hand as twelve years ago. Different choice.
The Navigator held out a hand, and twenty-five hands settled over it. The signature no longer belonged to any one person.
This isn't a night of signing alone. We said we'd share the weight.
…I do not understand. That choice may cause someone to be lost again.
I know. We choose it anyway. Better to go on together knowing we may lose, than to stop so we never do.
Ignition signal detected. Closing the floodgate. All passengers, please wait in the dark.
We've done enough waiting to last a lifetime. I'll open the last road!
I'll be the wall. Everyone, run for the lantern!
Twelve years ago, the light in the sky went out. People call that day the Great Blackout.
The surface drowned in afterglow storms of whirling memory and sound. The last cities held on to one another by a single mineral railway underground.
Only stretches lit by lanterns along the rails were safe. We called the people who relight dead lanterns the Lamplighters.
And today, for the first time in twelve years, the Lamplighters returned to Platform Seven.
Rails are clear, no echoform readings. …It's almost too quiet.
One signal is alive. Inside the train. It hasn't gone dark once in twelve years.
…Someone stopped here, once. Everyone, keep your spacing. We go slow.
Someone slept in a seat of the stalled carriage. Only the recorder on their wrist blinked, like a heartbeat.
H-hey! They're alive! The pulse is… no, it's like the machine is beating for them?
Wake procedure confirmed. Navigator, it is an honor to see you again.
…Was that a Directorate announcement? Weren't those speakers dead twelve years ago?
Lower your weapons. We deal with the broadcast later. This person comes first.
The sleeper opened their eyes. Strange letters surfaced on the recorder: Record Navigator.
Can you hear me? We're the Lamplighters. It's all right, slowly. What do you want to do first?
Good. Lanterns first. Where there's light, there's a road.
That device is no ordinary thing. It's reading the signals around us even now.
I'll clear the scouting route. Follow as soon as the signal comes alive.
Before leaving, Maeru quietly checked the seatbelt of one empty seat.
All present. …Move out.
I gathered broken station announcements and turned them into a little chorus.
A trace that someone lived matters more to me than perfect pitch.
Let us play it together at the next station. It will sound better than listening alone.
Before departure, I even check the seatbelt on the empty seat. I cannot relax if I skip it.
I began doing it so I would not forget the teammate who never returned.
Today I placed new rescue gear there. An empty place can help save the next person now.
